# Overview: What “leaching carbon loss” means

Leaching refers to the loss of carbon from soils and catchment stores when carbon dissolves or becomes entrained in water and is transported to streams, rivers, lakes, or groundwater, rather than remaining in the soil profile or being respired to CO2. Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) originates from the breakdown of plant litter, soil organic matter, and microbial byproducts, and can be exported via infiltration, surface runoff, and subsurface flow. Dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) arises from mineral weathering and microbial mineralization of organic carbon, and also enters waters through leaching and groundwater discharge. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Respiration and leaching are two main processes responsible for soil carbon loss</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-1">Most leached organic carbon in rainfall simulations is transported as particulate organic carbon via surface runoff, while dissolved organic carbon is significant in subsurface runoff and its composition shifts with antecedent moisture and rainfall intensity</cite>.

# Mechanisms and Pathways

Leaching losses emerge from three coupled mechanisms: production of dissolved carbon in soils, transport by hydrologic pathways, and processing or burial once in aquatic systems. <cite id="66cde1f-0">Soil is a major source of DOC entering streams; fluxes relate to soil carbon pools and are controlled by production, consumption, and transport through stream networks</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-1">Surface sealing under unsaturated, intense rainfall enhances runoff and POC export, whereas DOC dominates dissolved losses in surface flow and shows a concentrating effect under certain conditions</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Soil inorganic carbon is particularly prone to leaching during sporadic high precipitation events, and leaching has been under-constrained despite representing a notable fraction of soil carbon losses in some ecosystems</cite>.

In frozen and thawing landscapes, thaw reorganizes subsurface flow and exposes deep, labile carbon to weathering and microbial processing. <cite id="66d8d59a-1">Permafrost thaw increases groundwater circulation and mobilizes organic carbon from deep sediments (3–25 cm below surface), with DOC production, mineralization, and sorption governed by subsurface thermochemical conditions; peak mobilization can occur within two centuries of thaw initiation as supra-permafrost groundwater develops</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">Aged DOC and DIC can be transported to rivers as thaw liberates deeper carbon; more subsurface flow opens deep discharge pathways, increasing the export of older carbon</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-2">Thaw slumps dramatically increase particulate organic carbon delivery to streams, yet slump-mobilized POC shows minimal oxidation over a month in incubations, suggesting a strong fraction may be buried rather than mineralized</cite>.

Mineral weathering and redox chemistry add inorganic carbon to leaching fluxes. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Soil inorganic carbon is more leachable than organic carbon during high-intensity rainfall, highlighting mineral dissolution and carbonate mobilization as a route to DIC export</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-1">Freshwaters process 1.9–5.1 Pg C year−1, linking land to ocean via runoff, leaching through groundwater, and in-stream processing of dissolved carbon</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-4">Riverine organic carbon fluxes reflect terrestrial production and transport; dissolved organic carbon concentrations can be low where decomposition is rapid, while particulate forms dominate in some regions, and drainage intensity, basin slope, and soil carbon inputs govern fluxes</cite>.

# Quantitative Magnitude: Fluxes and Fractions

Leaching accounts for a non-negligible share of terrestrial carbon loss and export. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Across Europe, leaching of DOC from forests, grasslands, and croplands has been estimated at 15.1, 32.4, and 20.5 g C m−2 yr−1, representing 4%, 14%, and 8% of net ecosystem exchange, respectively</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-0">In upland organo-mineral UK soils, changes from grazed or semi-natural vegetation to forestry led to a 23% reduction in soil organic carbon where rainfall exceeded 1500 mm, implying losses via percolation and runoff that were not captured by depth sampling</cite>.

At farm and catchment scales, inputs and losses through hydrologic pathways can be large. <cite id="d59ed4a6-4">In temperate zones with ~500 mm rainfall, fields may receive 6.4–29.5 kg ha−1 of DOC in rainfall (1.28–5.9 mg L−1), and irrigation can add 4.6–30.8 kg ha−1; runoff and erosion can lose 0–1072 kg ha−1 yr−1, with eroded sediment showing organic carbon enrichment ratios of 0.39–5 and deep drainage containing up to 90 mg L−1 TOC; management (land use, tillage, slope, buffers) strongly influences losses</cite>.

Globally, leached DOC represents a significant fraction of terrestrial productivity and an important pathway to inland waters. <cite id="66cde14f-2">An integrative, observationally constrained modeling approach estimated a global terrestrial DOC leaching flux of 0.28 ± 0.07 Gt C year−1 from mineral soils, equivalent to about 15% of terrestrial Net Ecosystem Productivity, increasing to 22% in the tropics</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-3">From 1860 to 2010, global terrestrial DOC inputs to river networks increased by 35 Tg C year−1 (14%), with a 28% relative increase in boreal regions and a 9% increase in the tropics; runoff and DOC leaching show strong spatial and temporal correlation, and surface soil leaching contributes ~90% of total soil DOC leaching even though surface layers hold only ~40% of soil DOC stocks</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-1">Global inland waters process 1.9–5.1 Pg C year−1, underscoring the centrality of leaching and runoff in moving terrestrial dissolved carbon into aquatic systems</cite>.

For permafrost regions, thaw accelerates mobilization of ancient carbon. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">As permafrost thaws, older carbon stored in deeper soils and sediments is exposed to microbial and geochemical processes, increasing the transport of millennial-aged DOC and DIC to rivers via enhanced subsurface flow and groundwater discharge</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-1">Modeling suggests peak DOC mobilization from depths 3–25 m below the surface can precede complete permafrost loss, occurring within two centuries of thaw onset as supra-permafrost groundwater networks develop</cite>.

# Controls on Leaching Loss

Hydroclimate, vegetation inputs, and soil/bedrock chemistry regulate leaching losses. <cite id="d59ed4a6-1">Antecedent soil moisture and rainfall intensity control flow partitioning: under initially unsaturated conditions, surface sealing reduces infiltration and enhances runoff carrying most organic carbon as POC; rainfall intensity more strongly influences DOC losses, with DOC enriched in humic-like and protein-like fractions exported under certain conditions</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-0">High annual rainfall regimes show significant reductions in soil organic carbon, implicating leaching and runoff as important loss pathways even when bulk soil profiles show little vertical redistribution</cite>.

At regional scales, runoff and net primary production jointly control leaching. <cite id="66cde14f-3">Increases in DOC leaching over 1860–2010 correlate with a 15.5% increase in global runoff, with boreal regions showing the largest relative increase due to runoff changes, while temperate, subtropical, and tropical zones show larger increases driven by rising NPP with a secondary role for runoff</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-4">Inputs of DOC via rainfall and irrigation, along with soil losses through runoff and erosion, vary widely with management; deep drainage can carry dissolved carbon, including inorganic carbon, to groundwater and ultimately to surface waters</cite>.

In cold regions, thaw and terrain reorganization dominate controls. <cite id="66d8d59a-4">Retrogressive thaw slumps rapidly expose and mobilize previously frozen soils, increasing DOC delivery to streams; these features reshape landscapes and create strong coupling between permafrost degradation and carbon export</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">Warming increases mean active layer thickness and groundwater flow paths, elevating the discharge of older carbon from subsurface reservoirs into rivers</cite>.

Mineral chemistry and pH/redox conditions influence inorganic carbon losses and processing. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Soil inorganic carbon is more susceptible to leaching than organic carbon during high-intensity precipitation, pointing to mineral dissolution and transport of carbonate as a key DIC source to waters</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-1">Once in inland waters, 1.9–5.1 Pg C year−1 are processed, linking leached carbon to aquatic production, burial, and outgassing, with the fate of leached carbon depending on its bioavailability and transport timescales</cite>.

# Ecosystem Contrasts

Forests, grasslands, and croplands differ in leaching vulnerability and export pathways. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Forest soils leach about 15.1 g C m−2 yr−1 (4% of NEE), grasslands up to 32.4 g C m−2 yr−1 (14% of NEE), and croplands 20.5 g C m−2 yr−1 (8% of NEE), indicating that high-biomass ecosystems with active litter inputs and shallow rooting may lose larger fractions via leaching when hydrologic connectivity is high</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-1">In arable monoliths, POC dominates surface runoff and DOC is significant in subsurface flow; unsaturated, intense storms favor dissolved losses and distinct DOC composition, posing risks to aquatic ecosystems</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-0">High-rainfall upland systems show substantial SOC reductions where leaching and runoff exceed in-profile redistribution, especially on steep slopes</cite>.

Agriculture compounds risks by adding DOC and DIC through irrigation and by enhancing erosion. <cite id="d59ed4a6-4">Rainwater and irrigation can deliver 6.4–29.5 kg ha−1 of DOC (1.28–5.9 mg L−1) and 4.6–30.8 kg ha−1 of net carbon via irrigation water; runoff and erosion can remove 0–1072 kg ha−1 yr−1, with eroded sediments enriched in organic carbon and deep drainage carrying up to 90 mg L−1 total organic carbon; management (cover, slope, buffers) modulates losses</cite>.

Arctic and permafrost systems are especially sensitive to thaw-driven leaching. <cite id="66d8d59a-4">Thermokarst and retrogressive thaw slumps rapidly expose and transport previously frozen soils, making DOC a primary substrate for microbial mineralization to CO2 and a vehicle for terrestrial carbon to Arctic/Ocean sinks</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">As thaw deepens, older DOC and DIC from subsurface horizons enter rivers, elevating the age and mineralization potential of exported carbon</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-2">POC delivered from slumps shows low short-term mineralization, suggesting burial and adsorption may initially temper atmospheric CO2 feedbacks, though long-term fates depend on downstream processing and burial potential</cite>.

# Fate of Leached Carbon in Waters

Once exported, leached DOC and DIC undergo microbial processing, sorption, photodegradation, and burial, determining their climatic significance. <cite id="66cde14f-1">Global inland waters process 1.9–5.1 Pg C year−1, reflecting net transformation and transport of leached carbon from land to ocean</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-4">Riverine dissolved organic carbon concentrations can be low in tropical regions due to rapid decomposition, while particulate organic carbon can dominate fluxes in some regions; drainage intensity, basin slope, and soil carbon inputs are key determinants of DOC and POC fluxes</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">Thaw-exposed ancient DOC and DIC increase the biogeochemical influence of permafrost catchments, affecting river productivity and downstream DIC signatures</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-4">DOC acts as the primary substrate for microbial mineralization to CO2 and as the vehicle for terrestrial carbon to the Arctic Ocean, with implications from permafrost–carbon feedbacks to aquatic ecosystem functioning</cite>.

# Methods to Quantify Leaching Losses

Leaching is quantified through field measurements and models spanning soil, runoff, and groundwater pathways. <cite id="d59ed4a6-1">Rainfall simulation on undisturbed soil monoliths measures partitioning into surface and subsurface runoff and tracks dissolved and particulate carbon losses, including composition via photometric and fluorometric methods</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-4">On-farm hydrologic monitoring includes quantifying DOC and DIC inputs via rainfall and irrigation, and losses via runoff, erosion, and deep drainage; enrichment ratios in eroded sediments and concentrations in drainage water inform loss pathways</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-0">Catchment studies link soil DOC fluxes to soil carbon pools and stream transport, emphasizing the need to represent DOC production/export in land surface models to avoid overestimating carbon sequestration</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-2">Upscaling integrates sparse observations with process-based modeling to estimate global terrestrial DOC leaching (e.g., 0.28 ± 0.07 Gt C year−1 from mineral soils), highlighting the spatial bias of measurements toward industrialized regions</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-1">Virtual experiments and reactive transport models parameterize DOC mobilization and groundwater-borne export under permafrost thaw, identifying key biogeochemical parameters (e.g., DOC production, mineralization, sorption rates) that require field constraints</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-2">Stream incubations assess POC mineralization rates and sorption/adsorption protection, informing fates of thaw-delivered carbon in aquatic networks</cite>.

# Implications and Climate Feedbacks

Leaching links terrestrial carbon cycling with aquatic systems and climate through altered export, mineralization, and potential sequestration. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Leaching can rival 4–14% of ecosystem carbon uptake in some ecosystems, making it a first-order loss process alongside respiration</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-1">Leached carbon fuels substantial processing in inland waters (1.9–5.1 Pg C year−1), with outcomes for atmospheric CO2 depending on whether carbon is buried, remineralized, or exported to the ocean</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">In permafrost catchments, warming-driven thaw increases discharge of millennial-aged DOC and DIC to rivers via enhanced subsurface flow, amplifying both carbon loss and potential feedbacks to climate</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-4">Retrogressive thaw slumps increase POC delivery to streams, with evidence of low short-term mineralization and possible sediment burial, underscoring spatial and temporal heterogeneity in feedback strength</cite>.

# Key Uncertainties and Research Needs

Several gaps remain in quantifying and predicting leaching losses. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Soil carbon loss via leaching is relatively poorly constrained compared to respiration, despite recognized importance in high-rainfall and disturbed systems</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-1">Field data are lacking to constrain DOC production, bioavailability, and sorption in deep permafrost sediments and developing supra-permafrost groundwater systems, limiting predictive models of mobilization and export</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-1">Global maps of dissolved carbon in soil solution are lacking and drivers of DOC/DIC vary with landscape heterogeneity, complicating upscaling</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">The balance between microbial mineralization and sedimentation/burial of thaw-delivered carbon is uncertain, affecting permafrost–carbon feedback strength</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-4">Farm-scale empirical data on carbon loss through runoff, erosion, and deep drainage remain sparse, impeding accurate SOC balance predictions under management changes</cite>.

# Practical Management and Monitoring

Managing hydrologic connectivity and inputs can reduce leaching losses. <cite id="d59ed4a6-4">Practices such as changing land use, reduced tillage, maintaining ground cover, optimizing farm layout and slope, shortening furrow length, and using vegetative buffers can reduce carbon losses in runoff and erosion; rainfall/irrigation inputs of DOC and DIC should be monitored to avoid importing labile carbon that enhances leaching</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-1">On slopes and in high-intensity storm regimes, enhancing infiltration and reducing surface sealing (e.g., through cover and structure) can shift losses from surface runoff to subsurface pathways where DOC concentrations may be higher, requiring targeted protection of shallow soils</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-0">In high-rainfall regions, accounting for percolation and runoff losses is essential to avoid underestimating net SOC loss, especially on steep terrain</cite>.

# Summary

Leaching is a significant, often underappreciated pathway of carbon loss from soils and ecosystems, driven by hydroclimate, vegetation inputs, and subsurface flow, and it channels both modern and ancient carbon to aquatic systems where it is processed, stored, or released. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Across ecosystems, leaching losses of DOC can amount to 4–14% of net ecosystem exchange in forests and grasslands, with higher absolute fluxes in high-biomass systems</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-2">Globally, mineral soils leach roughly 0.28 ± 0.07 Gt DOC year−1, ~15% of terrestrial net productivity, with strong increases in boreal regions and elevated fractions in the tropics</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">Permafrost thaw accelerates mobilization of millennial-aged carbon to rivers by reactivating groundwater flow, potentially amplifying climate warming</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-1">Because inland waters process ~2–5 Pg C year−1, accurately representing leaching in models and monitoring exports at soil, catchment, and river-network scales is essential for reliable terrestrial carbon budgets and climate predictions</cite>.

Title: Antecedent soil moisture and rain intensity control pathways and quality of organic carbon exports from arable land
Snippet: Abstract Under conditions of climate change, the severity and probability of storm events and droughts are expected to increase, this may affect the partitioning into surface and subsurface runoff. However, there is still a debate on how such extreme weather conditions affect the leaching of soil organic carbon. The aim of this study was to ascertain the impact of rainfall intensity (63 vs 79 mm h−1) and antecedent soil moisture (Matric potential: −10 hPa vs −450 hPa) on flow partitioning in the transportation (fluxes and timing) of dissolved (DOC) and particulate organic carbon (POC). Rainfall simulation experiments using undisturbed soil monoliths (1 m × 0.5 m × 0.3 m) allowed to monitor the transport of water, sediments, DOC, and POC via surface and shallow subsurface runoff. In addition, the composition of the leached organic matter was analysed using photometric and fluorometric methods. Most of the organic carbon was transported as POC via surface runoff. In the surface runoff, the influence of antecedent soil moisture on POC loss was larger than rainfall intensity, while rainfall intensity had a greater influence on DOC losses. Under initially unsaturated conditions, surface sealing reduced the infiltration rate, thus fuelling the total surface runoff, which, in turn, enhanced the transported total sediment and POC load of the surface runoff. While POC dominated surface runoff, DOC played a crucial role in the subsurface runoff with higher DOC concentrations under unsaturated conditions. In contrast to other treatments, DOC exported from unsaturated soils rained with high intensity had a unique composition with the highest proportion of humic-like peaks (A, M, C), protein-like peaks (T) and components (C4), suggesting a concentrating effect on DOC at those soils. Altogether, this research acquires new insights into how flow partitioning under extreme weather conditions affects organic carbon losses and which transport mechanism might pose a risk for aquatic systems.

In this article, we review the Australian and global literature on terrestrial on farm carbon gains and losses in hydrological pathways. Catchment scale, landscape scale and modelling studies are not the focus of this review and are only briefly addressed. Carbon fractions associated with soil erosion and runoff include particulate organic and inorganic carbon, dissolved organic carbon (DOC), dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), dissolved CO 2 -C and dissolved CH 4 -C. Organic carbon enrichment ratios in eroded sediments range from 0.39 to 5. Total organic carbon concentrations in deep drainage below farming lands range from negligible to 90 mg L −1 . Title: Mobilization of subsurface carbon pools driven by permafrost thaw and reactivation of groundwater flow: a virtual experiment
Snippet: Permafrost thaw leads to an increase in groundwater circulation and potential mobilization of organic carbon sequestered in deep Arctic sediments (e.g. 3–25 m below surface). Upon thaw, a portion of this carbon may be transported along new groundwater flow paths to surface waters or be microbially transformed or immobilized by in-situ biogeochemical reactions. The fate of thaw-mobilized carbon impacts surface water productivity and global climate. We developed a numerical model to investigate the effects of subsurface warming, permafrost thaw, and resultant increased groundwater flow on the mobilization and reactive transport of dissolved organic carbon (DOC). Synthetic simulations demonstrate that mobilization and groundwater-borne DOC export are determined by subsurface thermo-chemical conditions that control the interplay of DOC production (organic matter degradation), mineralization, and sorption. Results suggest that peak carbon mobilization from these depths precedes complete permafrost loss, occurring within two centuries of thaw initiation with the development of supra-permafrost groundwater flow systems. Additionally, this study highlights the lack of field data needed to constrain these new models and apply them in real-word site-specific applications, specifically the amount and spatial variability of organic carbon in deep sediments and data to constrain DOC production rates for groundwater systems in degrading permafrost. Modeling results point to key biogeochemical parameters related to organic matter and carbon bioavailability to be measured in the field to bridge the gap between models and observations. This study provides a foundation for further developing a physics-based modeling framework to incorporate the influence of groundwater flow and permafrost thaw on permafrost DOC dynamics and export, which is imperative for advancing understanding and prediction of carbon release and terrestrial-aquatic carbon exchange in warming Artic landscapes in the coming decades.
</snippet>

Title: Low biodegradability of particulate organic carbon mobilized from thaw slumps on the Peel Plateau, NT, and possible chemosynthesis and sorption effects
Snippet: Abstract. Upon thaw, permafrost carbon entering streams may be mineralized into CO2 or re-sequestered into sediments. The balance between these processes is an important uncertainty in the permafrost-carbon-climate feedback. Warming and wetting in the western Canadian Arctic are accelerating thaw-driven mass wasting by permafrost thaw slumps, increasing particulate organic carbon (POC) delivered to headwater streams by orders of magnitude. Using aerobic incubations of POC from streams affected by thaw slumps we find that slump-mobilized POC undergoes minimal (~4 %) oxidation over a 1-month period and may be predominantly destined for sediment deposition. Mobilization of mineral-rich tills in this region may also protect carbon from mineralization via adsorption to minerals and promote inorganic carbon sequestration via chemolithoautotrophic processes. Region-specific assessments of permafrost carbon fates and inquiries beyond organic carbon decomposition are needed to constrain drivers of carbon cycling and climate feedbacks within stream networks affected by permafrost thaw.
</snippet>
<snippet id=66d8d59a-3>
Title: Warming and monsoonal climate lead to large export of millennial-aged carbon from permafrost catchments of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
Snippet: Permafrost thaw is another process governing the older carbon release (Schuur et al 2009, Aiken et al 2014). The term permafrost thaw is used to describe the transition of permafrost layer to seasonally thawed active layer under warming, which should not be confused with the active layer thaw at seasonal timescale. Spatially, the higher MAGT and thicker mean active layer thickness in the valley sites allows aged carbon release in deeper soil layer during summer. A higher degree of permafrost thaw liberates the aged carbon at the top of permafrost layer with subsurface flow, which results in ancient DOC transport in rivers (Vonk et al 2015). As permafrost thaws, the release of older carbonates in deeper soil layers or deep aquifers can also increase the DIC age in rivers (Barnes et al 2018). In the valley sites where MAGTs are higher, the potential for permafrost thaw is likely to be higher. Thereby, the sub-permafrost aquifer can discharge groundwater flow as more flow paths open (Walvoord and Kurylyk 2016), resulting in higher Q90/Q50 ratios (figure S3). More deep groundwater flow can bring older aged carbon to river water (figure 5). In the mountain sites, sub-permafrost groundwater flow is limited as a result of lower MAGT, which is suggested by the younger carbon age than that in the valley sites (figure 4). 

In addition to warming-induced active layer and permafrost thaw, we do not rule out other factors that can affect aged carbon sources. For instance, the long-range transport and deposition of black carbon from fossil fuel combustion (Li et al 2016, Yan et al 2019) may also fuel ancient organic carbon in river water via precipitation and runoff generation processes. The decomposition of thaw-released old soil organic carbon may produce 14 C-depleted CO 2 , which can weather minerals and enter river networks. Although we are unable to assess this effect on the DIC age due to the lack of soil 14 C-CO 2 data (Vaughn and Torn 2018).
</snippet>

Title: Retrogressive thaw slumps temper dissolved organic carbon delivery to streams of the Peel Plateau, NWT, Canada
Snippet: Within this context, the mobilization of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) from previously frozen soils is of particular interest because DOC acts as the primary substrate for the microbially mediated mineralization of organic carbon to carbon dioxide (Battin et al., 2008) and serves as the primary vehicle for the delivery of terrestrial carbon to the Arctic Ocean (Dittmar and Kattner, 2003;Holmes et al., 2012;Spencer et al., 2015). As a result, the implications of thaw-mediated DOC mobilization may range from effects on the permafrost-carbon feedback to the ecological and biogeochemical functioning of streams, rivers, and the nearshore ocean (e.g., Fritz et al., 2017;Tank et al., 2012a;Vonk et al., 2015a). 

Permafrost thaw can modify landscapes in many different ways, ranging from an increase in active-layer thickness and terrain subsidence to thermokarst features that significantly reconfigure the physical structure of landscapes (Kokelj and Jorgenson, 2013). Of these, thermokarst has the potential to rapidly expose significant quantities of previously frozen soils to biological and chemical processing (Abbott et al., 2014(Abbott et al., , 2015;;Malone et al., 2013;Tanski et al., 2017). One of the most conspicuous manifestations of thermokarst is the retrogressive thaw slump (RTS; Fig. 1), which develops as a result of mass wasting in ice-rich glacial deposits across northwestern Canada, Alaska, and western Siberia (Kokelj et al., 2017a) and in Yedoma regions of Alaska and Siberia (Murton et al., 2017). Thaw slumps are widespread throughout glaciated terrain in the western Canadian Arctic (Kokelj et al., 2017a;Lantuit et al., 2012), including on the Peel Plateau (Lacelle et al., 2015). These dynamic landforms develop via the ablation of an ice-rich headwall and are particularly efficient at thawing thick zones of ice-rich permafrost and translocating large volumes of sediment from slopes to downstream environments (see Fig. 1).

Title: Environmental Factors Influencing Dissolved Organic Carbon Concentrations in Afromontane Catchments
Snippet: Soil organic carbon (SOC) is a key component of the global carbon cycle. It is the largest terrestrial carbon pool (Liu et al. 2021;Tao et al. 2020) as it is estimated that the carbon contained in soil constitutes 75% of the total organic carbon stock stored in terrestrial ecosystems (Reyna-Bowen et al. 2019). Therefore, our ability to trace its path and residence time enhances our ability to study biogeochemical cycles and is essential for understanding the carbon cycle in terrestrial ecosystems (Wan et al. 2014). One of the crucial linkages between the land and ocean within the global carbon cycle is the transport of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) along streams and rivers (Jeong et al. 2012). The understanding of the dynamics of how DOC is processed and transported through stream networks is of importance as this organic carbon element is not only a master water quality variable in aquatic ecosystems (Ruhala and Zarnetske 2016) but is also a major contributor to the carbon budget of a catchment area (Rüegg et al. 2015). 

The majority of dissolved organic matter enters a stream by direct inputs from soils associated with the transport of surface water or groundwater, as only a small fraction of water typically enters a stream directly as rainfall (Aitkenhead-Peterson et al. 2003). The importance of soils in the fluxes of DOC in streams and rivers has therefore gained considerable interest, with many studies identifying that the fluxes of DOC relate to soil characteristics as well as the size of the soil carbon pool (Aitkenhead et al. 2007;Worrall et al. 2012). Many land surface models represent soils in a simplistic way and often neglect the production and export of DOC from soils to rivers. This leads to an overestimation of the potential carbon sequestration of a particular area, creating uncertainties in the predictions of the soil carbon response to land management changes as well as climate change (Camino-Serrano et al. 2018). Understanding the dynamics that control how DOC is exported from soils to aquatic systems is thus important for accurate estimations of carbon budgets (Camino-Serrano et al. 2018;Regnier et al. 2014). 

DOC export from ecosystems depends on its production and its consumption.
</snippet>

Title: Estimating dissolved carbon concentrations in global soils: a global database and model
Snippet: Terrestrial leached carbon (C) is commonly ignored in global C-cycle studies [1][2][3][4] leading to an inaccurate quantification of the terrestrial C budget [3,5]. Meanwhile, several studies show that leaching and transport through groundwater of dissolved C is a major C source to surface waters [6][7][8][9]. These freshwaters are important active systems in the global C cycle, linking the land and the ocean [10]. Global inland waters are estimated to process between 1.9 and 5.1 Pg C year −1 [11], indicating the magnitude of the C flux into streams, rivers, lakes and reservoirs is fraught with uncertainties [11][12][13][14]. This C flux from global terrestrial systems comprises litterfall from vegetation in floodplains and riparian zones of primarily headwaters, surface runoff, leaching from soils and processing via groundwater to surface waters. Several of these pathways exporting C from the land commence in soils [15,16]. The current study concerns C in this first part of the terrestrial-aquatic continuum: dissolved C in soil solution (soil pore water). 

A global spatially distributed estimate of dissolved C in soil solution may aid in the development of process-based global models (e.g. [17][18][19]) to constrain the C flux from terrestrial systems into inland waters [11,20,21]. However currently, global maps of dissolved C in soil solution are yet lacking. In the light of this knowledge gap, we address the following research questions: 

• How are dissolved C concentrations in soils spatially distributed on a global scale? • How can we make a spatially explicit first estimate of dissolved C concentrations in soils on a global scale, in order to constrain large-scale C fluxes from soils? 

Dissolved C in soil solution includes both organic (DOC) and inorganic C (DIC). In sampling studies, a range of factors has been identified as potential drivers of DOC and DIC concentrations in soil solutions. However landscape heterogeneity often implies that drivers at one location cannot be identified at another sampling plot.
</snippet>

Title: Leaching of dissolved organic carbon from mineral soils plays a significant role in the terrestrial carbon balance
Snippet: The leaching of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) from soils to the river network is an overlooked component of the terrestrial soil C budget. Measurements of DOC concentrations in soil, runoff and drainage are scarce and their spatial distribution highly skewed towards industrialized countries. The contribution of terrestrial DOC leaching to the global‐scale C balance of terrestrial ecosystems thus remains poorly constrained. Here, using a process based, integrative, modelling approach to upscale from existing observations, we estimate a global terrestrial DOC leaching flux of 0.28 ± 0.07 Gt C year−1 which is conservative, as it only includes the contribution of mineral soils. Our results suggest that globally about 15% of the terrestrial Net Ecosystem Productivity (NEP, calculated as the difference between Net Primary Production and soil respiration) is exported to aquatic systems as leached DOC. In the tropical rainforest, the leached fraction of terrestrial NEP even reaches 22%. Furthermore, we simulated spatial‐temporal trends in DOC leaching from soil to the river networks from 1860 to 2010. We estimated a global increase in terrestrial DOC inputs to river network of 35 Tg C year−1 (14%) from 1860 to 2010. Despite their low global contribution to the DOC leaching flux, boreal regions have the highest relative increase (28%) while tropics have the lowest relative increase (9%) over the historical period (1860s compared to 2000s). The results from our observationally constrained model approach demonstrate that DOC leaching is a significant flux in the terrestrial C budget at regional and global scales.
</snippet>

Title: Leaching of dissolved organic carbon from mineral soils plays a significant role in the terrestrial carbon balance
Snippet: For the period 1861-1870, we estimate an average global terrestrial DOC leaching of 250 Tg C year −1 , which then increases by 35 Tg C year −1 (14%; Figure 9b). Detailing these estimates per major climate zones, we simulated the highest relative increase of 28% in the boreal zone, followed by an increase of 22% in the temperate and 18% in the subtropical zones, and the lowest increase of 9% in the tropical zone (Figure 9). 

Our results show a concomitant increase in global runoff over the historical period of 15.5% (Table S5; Figure S9a) with a significant temporal and spatial correlation between runoff and DOC leaching (R 2 = 0.75 and 0.49 respectively), which can be explained by a strong transport limitation for DOC leaching flux from soils. 

However, the highest relative increase in DOC leaching in the Boreal zone is primarily due to the fact that here the highest increase in runoff is simulated, in line with a recent study in Sweden (Nydahl et. al., 2017). In contrast, the temperate, subtropical and tropical zones show an increase in DOC leaching which appears to be mainly driven by an increase in NPP (Table S4; Figure S9b) and only in the second place by an increase in runoff.

# Overview: What “leaching carbon loss” means

Leaching refers to the loss of carbon from soils and catchment stores when carbon dissolves or becomes entrained in water and is transported to streams, rivers, lakes, or groundwater, rather than remaining in the soil profile or being respired to CO2. Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) originates from the breakdown of plant litter, soil organic matter, and microbial byproducts, and can be exported via infiltration, surface runoff, and subsurface flow. Dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) arises from mineral weathering and microbial mineralization of organic carbon, and also enters waters through leaching and groundwater discharge. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Respiration and leaching are two main processes responsible for soil carbon loss</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-1">Most leached organic carbon in rainfall simulations is transported as particulate organic carbon via surface runoff, while dissolved organic carbon is significant in subsurface runoff and its composition shifts with antecedent moisture and rainfall intensity</cite>.

# Mechanisms and Pathways

Leaching losses emerge from three coupled mechanisms: production of dissolved carbon in soils, transport by hydrologic pathways, and processing or burial once in aquatic systems. <cite id="66cde1f-0">Soil is a major source of DOC entering streams; fluxes relate to soil carbon pools and are controlled by production, consumption, and transport through stream networks</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-1">Surface sealing under unsaturated, intense rainfall enhances runoff and POC export, whereas DOC dominates dissolved losses in surface flow and shows a concentrating effect under certain conditions</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Soil inorganic carbon is particularly prone to leaching during sporadic high precipitation events, and leaching has been under-constrained despite representing a notable fraction of soil carbon losses in some ecosystems</cite>.

In frozen and thawing landscapes, thaw reorganizes subsurface flow and exposes deep, labile carbon to weathering and microbial processing. <cite id="66d8d59a-1">Permafrost thaw increases groundwater circulation and mobilizes organic carbon from deep sediments (3–25 cm below surface), with DOC production, mineralization, and sorption governed by subsurface thermochemical conditions; peak mobilization can occur within two centuries of thaw initiation as supra-permafrost groundwater develops</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">Aged DOC and DIC can be transported to rivers as thaw liberates deeper carbon; more subsurface flow opens deep discharge pathways, increasing the export of older carbon</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-2">Thaw slumps dramatically increase particulate organic carbon delivery to streams, yet slump-mobilized POC shows minimal oxidation over a month in incubations, suggesting a strong fraction may be buried rather than mineralized</cite>.

Mineral weathering and redox chemistry add inorganic carbon to leaching fluxes. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Soil inorganic carbon is more leachable than organic carbon during high-intensity rainfall, highlighting mineral dissolution and carbonate mobilization as a route to DIC export</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-1">Freshwaters process 1.9–5.1 Pg C year−1, linking land to ocean via runoff, leaching through groundwater, and in-stream processing of dissolved carbon</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-4">Riverine organic carbon fluxes reflect terrestrial production and transport; dissolved organic carbon concentrations can be low where decomposition is rapid, while particulate forms dominate in some regions, and drainage intensity, basin slope, and soil carbon inputs govern fluxes</cite>.

# Quantitative Magnitude: Fluxes and Fractions

Leaching accounts for a non-negligible share of terrestrial carbon loss and export. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Across Europe, leaching of DOC from forests, grasslands, and croplands has been estimated at 15.1, 32.4, and 20.5 g C m−2 yr−1, representing 4%, 14%, and 8% of net ecosystem exchange, respectively</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-0">In upland organo-mineral UK soils, changes from grazed or semi-natural vegetation to forestry led to a 23% reduction in soil organic carbon where rainfall exceeded 1500 mm, implying losses via percolation and runoff that were not captured by depth sampling</cite>.

At farm and catchment scales, inputs and losses through hydrologic pathways can be large. <cite id="d59ed4a6-4">In temperate zones with ~500 mm rainfall, fields may receive 6.4–29.5 kg ha−1 of DOC in rainfall (1.28–5.9 mg L−1), and irrigation can add 4.6–30.8 kg ha−1; runoff and erosion can lose 0–1072 kg ha−1 yr−1, with eroded sediment showing organic carbon enrichment ratios of 0.39–5 and deep drainage containing up to 90 mg L−1 TOC; management (land use, tillage, slope, buffers) strongly influences losses</cite>.

Globally, leached DOC represents a significant fraction of terrestrial productivity and an important pathway to inland waters. <cite id="66cde14f-2">An integrative, observationally constrained modeling approach estimated a global terrestrial DOC leaching flux of 0.28 ± 0.07 Gt C year−1 from mineral soils, equivalent to about 15% of terrestrial Net Ecosystem Productivity, increasing to 22% in the tropics</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-3">From 1860 to 2010, global terrestrial DOC inputs to river networks increased by 35 Tg C year−1 (14%), with a 28% relative increase in boreal regions and a 9% increase in the tropics; runoff and DOC leaching show strong spatial and temporal correlation, and surface soil leaching contributes ~90% of total soil DOC leaching even though surface layers hold only ~40% of soil DOC stocks</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-1">Global inland waters process 1.9–5.1 Pg C year−1, underscoring the centrality of leaching and runoff in moving terrestrial dissolved carbon into aquatic systems</cite>.

For permafrost regions, thaw accelerates mobilization of ancient carbon. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">As permafrost thaws, older carbon stored in deeper soils and sediments is exposed to microbial and geochemical processes, increasing the transport of millennial-aged DOC and DIC to rivers via enhanced subsurface flow and groundwater discharge</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-1">Modeling suggests peak DOC mobilization from depths 3–25 m below the surface can precede complete permafrost loss, occurring within two centuries of thaw onset as supra-permafrost groundwater networks develop</cite>.

# Controls on Leaching Loss

Hydroclimate, vegetation inputs, and soil/bedrock chemistry regulate leaching losses. <cite id="d59ed4a6-1">Antecedent soil moisture and rainfall intensity control flow partitioning: under initially unsaturated conditions, surface sealing reduces infiltration and enhances runoff carrying most organic carbon as POC; rainfall intensity more strongly influences DOC losses, with DOC enriched in humic-like and protein-like fractions exported under certain conditions</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-0">High annual rainfall regimes show significant reductions in soil organic carbon, implicating leaching and runoff as important loss pathways even when bulk soil profiles show little vertical redistribution</cite>.

At regional scales, runoff and net primary production jointly control leaching. <cite id="66cde14f-3">Increases in DOC leaching over 1860–2010 correlate with a 15.5% increase in global runoff, with boreal regions showing the largest relative increase due to runoff changes, while temperate, subtropical, and tropical zones show larger increases driven by rising NPP with a secondary role for runoff</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-4">Inputs of DOC via rainfall and irrigation, along with soil losses through runoff and erosion, vary widely with management; deep drainage can carry dissolved carbon, including inorganic carbon, to groundwater and ultimately to surface waters</cite>.

In cold regions, thaw and terrain reorganization dominate controls. <cite id="66d8d59a-4">Retrogressive thaw slumps rapidly expose and mobilize previously frozen soils, increasing DOC delivery to streams; these features reshape landscapes and create strong coupling between permafrost degradation and carbon export</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">Warming increases mean active layer thickness and groundwater flow paths, elevating the discharge of older carbon from subsurface reservoirs into rivers</cite>.

Mineral chemistry and pH/redox conditions influence inorganic carbon losses and processing. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Soil inorganic carbon is more susceptible to leaching than organic carbon during high-intensity precipitation, pointing to mineral dissolution and transport of carbonate as a key DIC source to waters</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-1">Once in inland waters, 1.9–5.1 Pg C year−1 are processed, linking leached carbon to aquatic production, burial, and outgassing, with the fate of leached carbon depending on its bioavailability and transport timescales</cite>.

# Ecosystem Contrasts

Forests, grasslands, and croplands differ in leaching vulnerability and export pathways. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Forest soils leach about 15.1 g C m−2 yr−1 (4% of NEE), grasslands up to 32.4 g C m−2 yr−1 (14% of NEE), and croplands 20.5 g C m−2 yr−1 (8% of NEE), indicating that high-biomass ecosystems with active litter inputs and shallow rooting may lose larger fractions via leaching when hydrologic connectivity is high</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-1">In arable monoliths, POC dominates surface runoff and DOC is significant in subsurface flow; unsaturated, intense storms favor dissolved losses and distinct DOC composition, posing risks to aquatic ecosystems</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-0">High-rainfall upland systems show substantial SOC reductions where leaching and runoff exceed in-profile redistribution, especially on steep slopes</cite>.

Agriculture compounds risks by adding DOC and DIC through irrigation and by enhancing erosion. <cite id="d59ed4a6-4">Rainwater and irrigation can deliver 6.4–29.5 kg ha−1 of DOC (1.28–5.9 mg L−1) and 4.6–30.8 kg ha−1 of net carbon via irrigation water; runoff and erosion can remove 0–1072 kg ha−1 yr−1, with eroded sediments enriched in organic carbon and deep drainage carrying up to 90 mg L−1 total organic carbon; management (cover, slope, buffers) modulates losses</cite>.

Arctic and permafrost systems are especially sensitive to thaw-driven leaching. <cite id="66d8d59a-4">Thermokarst and retrogressive thaw slumps rapidly expose and transport previously frozen soils, making DOC a primary substrate for microbial mineralization to CO2 and a vehicle for terrestrial carbon to Arctic/Ocean sinks</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">As thaw deepens, older DOC and DIC from subsurface horizons enter rivers, elevating the age and mineralization potential of exported carbon</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-2">POC delivered from slumps shows low short-term mineralization, suggesting burial and adsorption may initially temper atmospheric CO2 feedbacks, though long-term fates depend on downstream processing and burial potential</cite>.

# Fate of Leached Carbon in Waters

Once exported, leached DOC and DIC undergo microbial processing, sorption, photodegradation, and burial, determining their climatic significance. <cite id="66cde14f-1">Global inland waters process 1.9–5.1 Pg C year−1, reflecting net transformation and transport of leached carbon from land to ocean</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-4">Riverine dissolved organic carbon concentrations can be low in tropical regions due to rapid decomposition, while particulate organic carbon can dominate fluxes in some regions; drainage intensity, basin slope, and soil carbon inputs are key determinants of DOC and POC fluxes</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">Thaw-exposed ancient DOC and DIC increase the biogeochemical influence of permafrost catchments, affecting river productivity and downstream DIC signatures</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-4">DOC acts as the primary substrate for microbial mineralization to CO2 and as the vehicle for terrestrial carbon to the Arctic Ocean, with implications from permafrost–carbon feedbacks to aquatic ecosystem functioning</cite>.

# Methods to Quantify Leaching Losses

Leaching is quantified through field measurements and models spanning soil, runoff, and groundwater pathways. <cite id="d59ed4a6-1">Rainfall simulation on undisturbed soil monoliths measures partitioning into surface and subsurface runoff and tracks dissolved and particulate carbon losses, including composition via photometric and fluorometric methods</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-4">On-farm hydrologic monitoring includes quantifying DOC and DIC inputs via rainfall and irrigation, and losses via runoff, erosion, and deep drainage; enrichment ratios in eroded sediments and concentrations in drainage water inform loss pathways</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-0">Catchment studies link soil DOC fluxes to soil carbon pools and stream transport, emphasizing the need to represent DOC production/export in land surface models to avoid overestimating carbon sequestration</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-2">Upscaling integrates sparse observations with process-based modeling to estimate global terrestrial DOC leaching (e.g., 0.28 ± 0.07 Gt C year−1 from mineral soils), highlighting the spatial bias of measurements toward industrialized regions</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-1">Virtual experiments and reactive transport models parameterize DOC mobilization and groundwater-borne export under permafrost thaw, identifying key biogeochemical parameters (e.g., DOC production, mineralization, sorption rates) that require field constraints</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-2">Stream incubations assess POC mineralization rates and sorption/adsorption protection, informing fates of thaw-delivered carbon in aquatic networks</cite>.

# Implications and Climate Feedbacks

Leaching links terrestrial carbon cycling with aquatic systems and climate through altered export, mineralization, and potential sequestration. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Leaching can rival 4–14% of ecosystem carbon uptake in some ecosystems, making it a first-order loss process alongside respiration</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-1">Leached carbon fuels substantial processing in inland waters (1.9–5.1 Pg C year−1), with outcomes for atmospheric CO2 depending on whether carbon is buried, remineralized, or exported to the ocean</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">In permafrost catchments, warming-driven thaw increases discharge of millennial-aged DOC and DIC to rivers via enhanced subsurface flow, amplifying both carbon loss and potential feedbacks to climate</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-4">Retrogressive thaw slumps increase POC delivery to streams, with evidence of low short-term mineralization and possible sediment burial, underscoring spatial and temporal heterogeneity in feedback strength</cite>.

# Key Uncertainties and Research Needs

Several gaps remain in quantifying and predicting leaching losses. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Soil carbon loss via leaching is relatively poorly constrained compared to respiration, despite recognized importance in high-rainfall and disturbed systems</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-1">Field data are lacking to constrain DOC production, bioavailability, and sorption in deep permafrost sediments and developing supra-permafrost groundwater systems, limiting predictive models of mobilization and export</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-1">Global maps of dissolved carbon in soil solution are lacking and drivers of DOC/DIC vary with landscape heterogeneity, complicating upscaling</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">The balance between microbial mineralization and sedimentation/burial of thaw-delivered carbon is uncertain, affecting permafrost–carbon feedback strength</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-4">Farm-scale empirical data on carbon loss through runoff, erosion, and deep drainage remain sparse, impeding accurate SOC balance predictions under management changes</cite>.

# Practical Management and Monitoring

Managing hydrologic connectivity and inputs can reduce leaching losses. <cite id="d59ed4a6-4">Practices such as changing land use, reduced tillage, maintaining ground cover, optimizing farm layout and slope, shortening furrow length, and using vegetative buffers can reduce carbon losses in runoff and erosion; rainfall/irrigation inputs of DOC and DIC should be monitored to avoid importing labile carbon that enhances leaching</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-1">On slopes and in high-intensity storm regimes, enhancing infiltration and reducing surface sealing (e.g., through cover and structure) can shift losses from surface runoff to subsurface pathways where DOC concentrations may be higher, requiring targeted protection of shallow soils</cite>. <cite id="d59ed4a6-0">In high-rainfall regions, accounting for percolation and runoff losses is essential to avoid underestimating net SOC loss, especially on steep terrain</cite>.

# Summary

Leaching is a significant, often underappreciated pathway of carbon loss from soils and ecosystems, driven by hydroclimate, vegetation inputs, and subsurface flow, and it channels both modern and ancient carbon to aquatic systems where it is processed, stored, or released. <cite id="d59ed4a6-3">Across ecosystems, leaching losses of DOC can amount to 4–14% of net ecosystem exchange in forests and grasslands, with higher absolute fluxes in high-biomass systems</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-2">Globally, mineral soils leach roughly 0.28 ± 0.07 Gt DOC year−1, ~15% of terrestrial net productivity, with strong increases in boreal regions and elevated fractions in the tropics</cite>. <cite id="66d8d59a-3">Permafrost thaw accelerates mobilization of millennial-aged carbon to rivers by reactivating groundwater flow, potentially amplifying climate warming</cite>. <cite id="66cde14f-1">Because inland waters process ~2–5 Pg C year−1, accurately representing leaching in models and monitoring exports at soil, catchment, and river-network scales is essential for reliable terrestrial carbon budgets and climate predictions</cite>.
</answer>

Snippet: Abstract Under conditions of climate change, the severity and probability of storm events and droughts are expected to increase, this may affect the partitioning into surface and subsurface runoff. While POC dominated surface runoff, DOC played a crucial role in the subsurface runoff with higher DOC concentrations under unsaturated conditions. In contrast to other treatments, DOC exported from unsaturated soils rained with high intensity had a unique composition with the highest proportion of humic-like peaks (A, M, C), protein-like peaks (T) and components (C4), suggesting a concentrating effect on DOC at those soils. Altogether, this research acquires new insights into how flow partitioning under extreme weather conditions affects organic carbon losses and which transport mechanism might pose a risk for aquatic systems.

Title: Age and chemistry of dissolved organic carbon reveal enhanced leaching of ancient labile carbon at the permafrost thaw zone
Snippet: No content available

Title: Mobilization of subsurface carbon pools driven by permafrost thaw and reactivation of groundwater flow: a virtual experiment
Snippet: Permafrost thaw leads to an increase in groundwater circulation and potential mobilization of organic carbon sequestered in deep Arctic sediments (e.g. 3–25 m below surface). Upon thaw, a portion of this carbon may be transported along new groundwater flow paths to surface waters or be microbially transformed or immobilized by in-situ biogeochemical reactions. The fate of thaw-mobilized carbon impacts surface water productivity and global climate. We developed a numerical model to investigate the effects of subsurface warming, permafrost thaw, and resultant increased groundwater flow on the mobilization and reactive transport of dissolved organic carbon (DOC). Synthetic simulations demonstrate that mobilization and groundwater-borne DOC export are determined by subsurface thermo-chemical conditions that control the interplay of DOC production (organic matter degradation), mineralization, and sorption. Results suggest that peak carbon mobilization from these depths precedes complete permafrost loss, occurring within two centuries of thaw initiation with the development of supra-permafrost groundwater flow systems. Additionally, this study highlights the lack of field data needed to constrain these new models and apply them in real-word site-specific applications, specifically the amount and spatial variability of organic carbon in deep sediments and data to constrain DOC production rates for groundwater systems in degrading permafrost. Modeling results point to key biogeochemical parameters related to organic matter and carbon bioavailability to be measured in the field to bridge the gap between models and observations. This study provides a foundation for further developing a physics-based modeling framework to incorporate the influence of groundwater flow and permafrost thaw on permafrost DOC dynamics and export, which is imperative for advancing understanding and prediction of carbon release and terrestrial-aquatic carbon exchange in warming Artic landscapes in the coming decades.

Title: Low biodegradability of particulate organic carbon mobilized from thaw slumps on the Peel Plateau, NT, and possible chemosynthesis and sorption effects
Snippet: Abstract. Upon thaw, permafrost carbon entering streams may be mineralized into CO2 or re-sequestered into sediments. The balance between these processes is an important uncertainty in the permafrost-carbon-climate feedback. Warming and wetting in the western Canadian Arctic are accelerating thaw-driven mass wasting by permafrost thaw slumps, increasing particulate organic carbon (POC) delivered to headwater streams by orders of magnitude. Using aerobic incubations of POC from streams affected by thaw slumps we find that slump-mobilized POC undergoes minimal (~4 %) oxidation over a 1-month period and may be predominantly destined for sediment deposition. Mobilization of mineral-rich tills in this region may also protect carbon from mineralization via adsorption to minerals and promote inorganic carbon sequestration via chemolithoautotrophic processes. Region-specific assessments of permafrost carbon fates and inquiries beyond organic carbon decomposition are needed to constrain drivers of carbon cycling and climate feedbacks within stream networks affected by permafrost thaw.

Title: Warming and monsoonal climate lead to large export of millennial-aged carbon from permafrost catchments of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
Snippet: Permafrost thaw is another process governing the older carbon release (Schuur et al 2009, Aiken et al 2014). The term permafrost thaw is used to describe the transition of permafrost layer to seasonally thawed active layer under warming, which should not be confused with the active layer thaw at seasonal timescale. Spatially, the higher MAGT and thicker mean active layer thickness in the valley sites allows aged carbon release in deeper soil layer during summer. A higher degree of permafrost thaw liberates the aged carbon at the top of permafrost layer with subsurface flow, which results in ancient DOC transport in rivers (Vonk et al 2015). As permafrost thaws, the release of older carbonates in deeper soil layers or deep aquifers can also increase the DIC age in rivers (Barnes et al 2018). In the valley sites where MAGTs are higher, the potential for permafrost thaw is likely to be higher. Thereby, the sub-permafrost aquifer can discharge groundwater flow as more flow paths open (Walvoord and Kurylyk 2016), resulting in higher Q90/Q50 ratios (figure S3). More deep groundwater flow can bring older aged carbon to river water (figure 5). In the mountain sites, sub-permafrost groundwater flow is limited as a result of lower MAGT, which is suggested by the younger carbon age than that in the valley sites (figure 4). 

In addition to warming-induced active layer and permafrost thaw, we do not rule out other factors that can affect aged carbon sources. For instance, the long-range transport and deposition of black carbon from fossil fuel combustion (Li et al 2016, Yan et al 2019) may also fuel ancient organic carbon in river water via precipitation and runoff generation processes. The decomposition of thaw-released old soil organic carbon may produce 14 C-depleted CO 2 , which can weather minerals and enter river networks. Although we are unable to assess this effect on the DIC age due to the lack of soil 14 C-CO 2 data (Vaughn and Torn 2018).

Title: Retrogressive thaw slumps temper dissolved organic carbon delivery to streams of the Peel Plateau, NWT, Canada
Snippet: Within this context, the mobilization of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) from previously frozen soils is of particular interest because DOC acts as the primary substrate for the microbially mediated mineralization of organic carbon to carbon dioxide (Battin et al., 2008) and serves as the primary vehicle for the delivery of terrestrial carbon to the Arctic Ocean (Dittmar and Kattner, 2003;Holmes et al., 2012;Spencer et al., 2015). As a result, the implications of thaw-mediated DOC mobilization may range from effects on the permafrost-carbon feedback to the ecological and biogeochemical functioning of streams, rivers, and the nearshore ocean (e.g., Fritz et al., 2017;Tank et al., 2012a;Vonk et al., 2015a). 

Permafrost thaw can modify landscapes in many different ways, ranging from an increase in active-layer thickness and terrain subsidence to thermokarst features that significantly reconfigure the physical structure of landscapes (Kokelj and Jorgenson, 2013). Of these, thermokarst has the potential to rapidly expose significant quantities of previously frozen soils to biological and chemical processing (Abbott et al., 2014(Abbott et al., , 2015;;Malone et al., 2013;Tanski et al., 2017). One of the most conspicuous manifestations of thermokarst is the retrogressive thaw slump (RTS; Fig. 1), which develops as a result of mass wasting in ice-rich glacial deposits across northwestern Canada, Alaska, and western Siberia (Kokelj et al., 2017a) and in Yedoma regions of Alaska and Siberia (Murton et al., 2017). Thaw slumps are widespread throughout glaciated terrain in the western Canadian Arctic (Kokelj et al., 2017a;Lantuit et al., 2012), including on the Peel Plateau (Lacelle et al., 2015). These dynamic landforms develop via the ablation of an ice-rich headwall and are particularly efficient at thawing thick zones of ice-rich permafrost and translocating large volumes of sediment from slopes to downstream environments (see Fig. 1).

Permafrost thaw is another process governing the older carbon release (Schuur et al 2009, Aiken et al 2014). The term permafrost thaw is used to describe the transition of permafrost layer to seasonally thawed active layer under warming, which should not be confused with the active layer thaw at seasonal timescale. Spatially, the higher MAGT and thicker mean active layer thickness in the valley sites allows aged carbon release in deeper soil layer during summer. A higher degree of permafrost thaw liberates the aged carbon at the top of permafrost layer with subsurface flow, which results in ancient DOC transport in rivers (Vonk et al 2015). As permafrost thaws, the release of older carbonates in deeper soil layers or deep aquifers can also increase the DIC age in rivers (Barnes et al 2018). In the valley sites where MAGTs are higher, the potential for permafrost thaw is likely to be higher. Thereby, the sub-permafrost aquifer can discharge groundwater flow as more flow paths open (Walvoord and Kurylyk 2016), resulting in higher Q90/Q50 ratios (figure S3). More deep groundwater flow can bring older aged carbon to river water (figure 5). In the mountain sites, sub-permafrost groundwater flow is limited as a result of lower MAGT, which is suggested by the younger carbon age than that in the valley sites (figure 4). 

In addition to warming-induced active layer and permafrost thaw, we do not rule out other factors that can affect aged carbon sources. For instance, the long-range transport and deposition of black carbon from fossil fuel combustion (Li et al 2016, Yan et al 2019) may also fuel ancient organic carbon in river water via precipitation and runoff generation processes. The decomposition of thaw-released old soil organic carbon may produce 14 C-depleted CO 2 , which can weather minerals and enter river networks. Although we are unable to assess this effect on the DIC age due to the lack of soil 14 C-CO 2 data (Vaughn and Torn 2018).

Within this context, the mobilization of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) from previously frozen soils is of particular interest because DOC acts as the primary substrate for the microbially mediated mineralization of organic carbon to carbon dioxide (Battin et al., 2008) and serves as the primary vehicle for the delivery of terrestrial carbon to the Arctic Ocean (Dittmar and Kattner, 2003;Holmes et al., 2012;Spencer et al., 2015). As a result, the implications of thaw-mediated DOC mobilization may range from effects on the permafrost-carbon feedback to the ecological and biogeochemical functioning of streams, rivers, and the nearshore ocean (e.g., Fritz et al., 2017;Tank et al., 2012a;Vonk et al., 2015a). 

Permafrost thaw can modify landscapes in many different ways, ranging from an increase in active-layer thickness and terrain subsidence to thermokarst features that significantly reconfigure the physical structure of landscapes (Kokelj and Jorgenson, 2013). Of these, thermokarst has the potential to rapidly expose significant quantities of previously frozen soils to biological and chemical processing (Abbott et al., 2014(Abbott et al., , 2015;;Malone et al., 2013;Tanski et al., 2017). One of the most conspicuous manifestations of thermokarst is the retrogressive thaw slump (RTS; Fig. 1), which develops as a result of mass wasting in ice-rich glacial deposits across northwestern Canada, Alaska, and western Siberia (Kokelj et al., 2017a) and in Yedoma regions of Alaska and Siberia (Murton et al., 2017). Thaw slumps are widespread throughout glaciated terrain in the western Canadian Arctic (Kokelj et al., 2017a;Lantuit et al., 2012), including on the Peel Plateau (Lacelle et al., 2015). These dynamic landforms develop via the ablation of an ice-rich headwall and are particularly efficient at thawing thick zones of ice-rich permafrost and translocating large volumes of sediment from slopes to downstream environments (see Fig. 1).

documents.snippet: Permafrost thaw leads to an increase in groundwater circulation and potential mobilization of organic carbon sequestered in deep Arctic sediments (e.g. 3–25 m below surface). Upon thaw, a portion of this carbon may be transported along new groundwater flow paths to surface waters or be microbially transformed or immobilized by in-situ biogeochemical reactions. The fate of thaw-mobilized carbon impacts surface water productivity and global climate. We developed a numerical model to investigate the effects of subsurface warming, permafrost thaw, and resultant increased groundwater flow on the mobilization and reactive transport of dissolved organic carbon (DOC). Synthetic simulations demonstrate that mobilization and groundwater-borne DOC export are determined by subsurface thermo-chemical conditions that control the interplay of DOC production (organic matter degradation), mineralization, and sorption. Results suggest that peak carbon mobilization from these depths precedes complete permafrost loss, occurring within two centuries of thaw initiation with the development of supra-permafrost groundwater flow systems. Additionally, this study highlights the lack of field data needed to constrain these new models and apply them in real-word site-specific applications, specifically the amount and spatial variability of organic carbon in deep sediments and data to constrain DOC production rates for groundwater systems in degrading permafrost. Modeling results point to key biogeochemical parameters related to organic matter and carbon bioavailability to be measured in the field to bridge the gap between models and observations. This study provides a foundation for further developing a physics-based modeling framework to incorporate the influence of groundwater flow and permafrost thaw on permafrost DOC dynamics and export, which is imperative for advancing understanding and prediction of carbon release and terrestrial-aquatic carbon exchange in warming Artic landscapes in the coming decades.

Title: Environmental Factors Influencing Dissolved Organic Carbon Concentrations in Afromontane Catchments
Snippet: Soil organic carbon (SOC) is a key component of the global carbon cycle. It is the largest terrestrial carbon pool (Liu et al. 2021;Tao et al. 2020) as it is estimated that the carbon contained in soil constitutes 75% of the total organic carbon stock stored in terrestrial ecosystems (Reyna-Bowen et al. 2019). Therefore, our ability to trace its path and residence time enhances our ability to study biogeochemical cycles and is essential for understanding the carbon cycle in terrestrial ecosystems (Wan et al. 2014). One of the crucial linkages between the land and ocean within the global carbon cycle is the transport of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) along streams and rivers (Jeong et al. 2012). The understanding of the dynamics of how DOC is processed and transported through stream networks is of importance as this organic carbon element is not only a master water quality variable in aquatic ecosystems (Ruhala and Zarnetske 2016) but is also a major contributor to the carbon budget of a catchment area (Rüegg et al. 2015). 

The majority of dissolved organic matter enters a stream by direct inputs from soils associated with the transport of surface water or groundwater, as only a small fraction of water typically enters a stream directly as rainfall (Aitkenhead-Peterson et al. 2003). The importance of soils in the fluxes of DOC in streams and rivers has therefore gained considerable interest, with many studies identifying that the fluxes of DOC relate to soil characteristics as well as the size of the soil carbon pool (Aitkenhead et al. 2007;Worrall et al. 2012). Many land surface models represent soils in a simplistic way and often neglect the production and export of DOC from soils to rivers. This leads to an overestimation of the potential carbon sequestration of a particular area, creating uncertainties in the predictions of the soil carbon response to land management changes as well as climate change (Camino-Serrano et al. 2018). Understanding the dynamics that control how DOC is exported from soils to aquatic systems is thus important for accurate estimations of carbon budgets (Camino-Serrano et al. 2018;Regnier et al. 2014). 

DOC export from ecosystems depends on its production and its consumption.

Title: Estimating dissolved carbon concentrations in global soils: a global database and model
Snippet: Terrestrial leached carbon (C) is commonly ignored in global C-cycle studies [1][2][3][4] leading to an inaccurate quantification of the terrestrial C budget [3,5]. Meanwhile, several studies show that leaching and transport through groundwater of dissolved C is a major C source to surface waters [6][7][8][9]. These freshwaters are important active systems in the global C cycle, linking the land and the ocean [10]. Global inland waters are estimated to process between 1.9 and 5.1 Pg C year −1 [11], indicating the magnitude of the C flux into streams, rivers, lakes and reservoirs is fraught with uncertainties [11][12][13][14]. This C flux from global terrestrial systems comprises litterfall from vegetation in floodplains and riparian zones of primarily headwaters, surface runoff, leaching from soils and processing via groundwater to surface waters. Several of these pathways exporting C from the land commence in soils [15,16]. The current study concerns C in this first part of the terrestrial-aquatic continuum: dissolved C in soil solution (soil pore water). 

A global spatially distributed estimate of dissolved C in soil solution may aid in the development of process-based global models (e.g. [17][18][19]) to constrain the C flux from terrestrial systems into inland waters [11,20,21]. However currently, global maps of dissolved C in soil solution are yet lacking. In the light of this knowledge gap, we address the following research questions: 

• How are dissolved C concentrations in soils spatially distributed on a global scale? • How can we make a spatially explicit first estimate of dissolved C concentrations in soils on a global scale, in order to constrain large-scale C fluxes from soils? 

Dissolved C in soil solution includes both organic (DOC) and inorganic C (DIC). In sampling studies, a range of factors has been identified as potential drivers of DOC and DIC concentrations in soil solutions. However landscape heterogeneity often implies that drivers at one location cannot be identified at another sampling plot.

Title: Leaching of dissolved organic carbon from mineral soils plays a significant role in the terrestrial carbon balance
Snippet: The leaching of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) from soils to the river network is an overlooked component of the terrestrial soil C budget. Measurements of DOC concentrations in soil, runoff and drainage are scarce and their spatial distribution highly skewed towards industrialized countries. The contribution of terrestrial DOC leaching to the global‐scale C balance of terrestrial ecosystems thus remains poorly constrained. Here, using a process based, integrative, modelling approach to upscale from existing observations, we estimate a global terrestrial DOC leaching flux of 0.28 ± 0.07 Gt C year−1 which is conservative, as it only includes the contribution of mineral soils. Our results suggest that globally about 15% of the terrestrial Net Ecosystem Productivity (NEP, calculated as the difference between Net Primary Production and soil respiration) is exported to aquatic systems as leached DOC. In the tropical rainforest, the leached fraction of terrestrial NEP even reaches 22%. Furthermore, we simulated spatial‐temporal trends in DOC leaching from soil to the river networks from 1860 to 2010. We estimated a global increase in terrestrial DOC inputs to river network of 35 Tg C year−1 (14%) from 1860 to 2010. Despite their low global contribution to the DOC leaching flux, boreal regions have the highest relative increase (28%) while tropics have the lowest relative increase (9%) over the historical period (1860s compared to 2000s). The results from our observationally constrained model approach demonstrate that DOC leaching is a significant flux in the terrestrial C budget at regional and global scales.

Title: Leaching of dissolved organic carbon from mineral soils plays a significant role in the terrestrial carbon balance
Snippet: For the period 1861-1870, we estimate an average global terrestrial DOC leaching of 250 Tg C year −1 , which then increases by 35 Tg C year −1 (14%; Figure 9b). Detailing these estimates per major climate zones, we simulated the highest relative increase of 28% in the boreal zone, followed by an increase of 22% in the temperate and 18% in the subtropical zones, and the lowest increase of 9% in the tropical zone (Figure 9). 

Our results show a concomitant increase in global runoff over the historical period of 15.5% (Table S5; Figure S9a) with a significant temporal and spatial correlation between runoff and DOC leaching (R 2 = 0.75 and 0.49 respectively), which can be explained by a strong transport limitation for DOC leaching flux from soils. 

However, the highest relative increase in DOC leaching in the Boreal zone is primarily due to the fact that here the highest increase in runoff is simulated, in line with a recent study in Sweden (Nydahl et. al., 2017). In contrast, the temperate, subtropical and tropical zones show an increase in DOC leaching which appears to be mainly driven by an increase in NPP (Table S4; Figure S9b) and only in the second place by an increase in runoff.

DOC, net primary production (NPP) and net ecosystem productivity (NEP) and export ratios  Over the simulation period, surface soil leaching contributes about 90% to total DOC leaching from soil. Title: Hydro-ecological controls on riverine organic carbon dynamics in the tropical monsoon region
Snippet: As the key channel linking marine and terrestrial ecosystem, global rivers played an important role on the global carbon cycle 1,2 . According to previous statistics, about 1Gt C were annually transported into the ocean via global rivers 3 , accounting for 20% of the total absorption amount (5.0Gt) in terrestrial and marine ecosystem (http:// co2now.org). In the fluvial fluxes, the 40% were transported in the form of organic carbon by global rivers 4 , approximating to 1~2% of the net primary production 5 . While, the riverine organic carbon concentrations and their output process reflected terrestrial ecosystem changes, and the fluxes exported into the ocean were the important constraint of the oceanic carbon budget and cycling 6 . In previous research, two approaches that carbon data for large rivers and the model formulas were recognized to estimate global riverine carbon fluxes 7 . In the former, the measured data of riverine organic carbon concentrations in various regions was particularly important, considering that there were large differences in river organic carbon concentrations in different latitudes regions 1 . The available studies research certificated that the riverine dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations were not high in the tropical regions due to the rapidly decomposition of organic matters, in spite of high primary productivities 1 . However, Huang et al. had pointed out that the total fluxes of riverine organic carbon in the Asia area kept at a much higher level 7 . It was possible that particulate organic carbon (POC), which was carried by particulate suspension, occupied a large proportion, but enough supporting materials should be provided. In the latter, the parameters applied for establishing fluvial fluxes models were sometimes regional, which hardly represented the overall situation of global rivers. As the results concluded by Ludwig et al., the drainage intensity, basin slope and amount of organic soil carbon were the main determinants of DOC fluxes and the total mass of suspended matter govern POC fluxes 4 .
