Summary
Leached dissolved organic carbon (DOC)—the soluble organic fraction exported from soils and catchments into rivers, estuaries, and coastal waters—does not follow uniform mineralization kinetics across aquatic systems. Instead, rates and pathways are strongly structured by the chemical and molecular composition of the terrestrial DOM, by microbial community and environmental controls (light, temperature, nutrients, redox), and by hydrodynamics at the land–sea interface. As a result, predicting terrestrial carbon loss from DOC hinges on resolving DOM quality and site context rather than assuming a single, transferable kinetic constant across systems. <cite id="ee65992e-0">Estuaries integrate allochthonous and autochthonous organic matter and modify it via flocculation, sinking, photolysis, and microbial degradation, so DOM components (including DOC) have different fates shaped by composition and environmental interactions</cite> <cite id="ee65992e-2">Variation in DOM quality can explain up to 75% of the variability in bacterial growth in estuarine waters, with bacterial growth efficiency inversely related to the DOC: DON ratio and influenced by multiple environmental variables</cite> <cite id="ee65992e-3">Across >200 lakes, sunlight-dominated processing of DOC was found, with photomineralization averaging 5× greater than dark bacterial respiration; predicting DOC reactivity has been challenging</cite> <cite id="187ac718-0">Autochthonous DOM is generally more aliphatic, lower molecular weight, and more bioavailable, whereas natural allochthonous DOM is more aromatic, higher molecular weight, and less bioavailable</cite>.

Why kinetics are heterogeneous
1) Molecular and optical composition of leached DOM. <cite id="187ac718-0">Terrestrial (allochthonous) DOM is enriched in aromatic, high–molecular weight compounds and tends to be less bioavailable than autochthonous DOM, which is lower in aromaticity and molecular weight and more bioavailable</cite>. <cite id="ee65992e-0">In estuaries, optical properties (absorbance and fluorescence of chromophoric DOM) track source and composition; DOM components have different fates depending on elemental stoichiometry and interactions with biotic and abiotic factors</cite>. <cite id="9ea9bbc4-0">Photomineralization of terrestrially derived DOC is a major removal pathway; for example, in the Rio Negro tributary of the Amazon, ~15% of DOC became photoreactive after 27 h of sunlight exposure and photomineralization rates (~4.0 μM hr−1) exceeded bacterial utilization by ~7×, with photomineralization accounting for 70–90% of water-column DOC processing in Arctic lakes and rivers</cite>. <cite id="9ea9bbc4-0">Photodegradation can decrease color (absorbance) and molecular weight of DOC, increasing light availability and subsequent bacterial respiration</cite>. Together these show that the same “leached” DOC is a heterogeneous mixture of reactive classes whose lability and pathway partitioning depend on chemistry and evolving exposure to light.

2) Partitioning between photochemical and microbial pathways. <cite id="ee65992e-3">Traditional views emphasized bacterial respiration as dominant, but large-scale surveys of Arctic lakes, rivers, and streams found sunlight-dominated processing, with average photomineralization 5× greater than dark respiration</cite>. <cite id="9ea9bbc4-2">In a eutrophic, semiarid estuary (Baffin Bay, Texas), first-order photoproduction of dissolved inorganic carbon ranged from 0.16 to 0.68 μM hr−1, corresponding to daily DOC removal of 0.3–1.5% of standing stock, with photomineralization negatively correlated with chlorophyll a (plankton-derived DOC less photoreactive) and DIC Keeling plots indicating high lability of 13C-enriched (terrestrial-like) DOC</cite>. <cite id="9ea9bbc4-1">In the Tyne estuary, extrapolation from CO photoproduction suggested DOC removal via photoproduction amounted to 0.004–0.014% of total riverine DOC inputs, with total photochemical losses of DOC ~0.13–0.46% of inputs</cite>. These contrasts across systems demonstrate that the balance between photochemical and microbial routes varies with DOM optical chemistry, trophic state, and light exposure, so kinetics cannot be assumed uniform.

3) Microbial processing and growth efficiency controls. <cite id="ee65992e-2">Bacterial growth efficiency (BGE) is strongly shaped by DOM quality; higher DOC: DON ratios are typically associated with lower BGE, and BGE depends on light, nutrients, temperature, and other environmental variables</cite>. <cite id="ee65992e-4">Bacterial carbon demand and the partitioning between production and respiration vary spatially and temporally due to temperature, inorganic nutrients, DOM quality, light, and grazing, necessitating simultaneous measurements of bacterial production and respiration to capture carbon metabolism and its regulation</cite>. Because BGE and microbial carbon demand co-determine carbon loss through respiration from any given DOC flux, kinetic expectations shift with environmental context and DOM quality, precluding a single universal rate.

4) Estuarine mixing and coastal transformation. <cite id="ee65992e-0">Estuaries receive both allochthonous and autochthonous inputs and process DOM via flocculation, sinking, photolysis, and microbial degradation; DOM components may have different fates depending on composition and biotic/abiotic interactions</cite>. <cite id="ee65992e-2">Rivers deliver an order of magnitude order of magnitude 0.25 Gt of dissolved organic carbon to the ocean annually; variation in DOM quality linked to catchment land use alters bacterial utilization, implying that leached DOC’s fate depends on catchment-derived composition</cite>. <cite id="9ea9bbc4-0">Photomineralization converts DOC to dissolved inorganic carbon in coastal and open-ocean waters and can enhance biomineralization by ~50% in a large river-influenced margin, indicating that terrestrial DOM can be rapidly processed photochemically even offshore</cite>. These coastal linkages show that leached DOC’s mineralization kinetics are filtered through estuarine and oceanic physical–biogeochemical dynamics, adding system-specific variability.

Predictability: what can be forecast and what cannot
- Testable constraints and models. <cite id="ee65992e-2">DOM quality explains a large fraction of bacterial growth variability, enabling models and management to anticipate microbial processing when composition (e.g., absorbance, fluorescence, DOC: DON) is measured</cite>. <cite id="187ac718-0">Empirical generalizations of DOM chemistry—more aromatic, higher molecular weight allochthonous DOM tending to be less bioavailable—provide transferable predictors of initial lability and potential mineralization pathways</cite>. <cite id="9ea9bbc4-0">Because photodegradation can increase lability (lower molecular weight, less colored DOC), optical tracers of CDOM/fDOM can forecast both direct mineralization and subsequent enhanced biomineralization</cite>. <cite id="ee65992e-2">Catchment land use alters DOM quality and thus bacterial growth and BGE, suggesting that watershed characterization can improve predictions of downstream carbon processing</cite>. In practice, this means that if the optical/chemical “size classes” of leached DOC are resolved, first-order mineralization kinetics can be parameterized locally with acceptable predictive skill, but a universal constant is unlikely to transfer across catchments.

- Limits to predictability and sources of uncertainty. <cite id="ee65992e-3">Despite these predictors, large surveys show that predicting DOC reactivity remains challenging and that sunlight-dominated processing can flip kinetic expectations relative to traditional dark-biomineralization paradigms</cite>. <cite id="ee65992e-4">Bacterial production and respiration co-vary with temperature, nutrients, light, DOM quality, and grazing, so even well-constrained compositions can yield different carbon losses depending on concurrent environmental states</cite>. <cite id="187ac718-0">Wetlands and treatment systems can shift net DOM processing via microbial mineralization and photodegradation, with anaerobic conditions restricting mineralization efficiency but enhancing removal via denitrification, sedimentation, and sorption</cite>. <cite id="187ac718-2">Salinity and hydrology modulate decomposition and burial; higher salinity often accelerates sulfate-driven turnover and carbon turnover, whereas low-salinity tidal marshes can show suppressed decomposition and greater carbon stocks, demonstrating strong coastal gradients in mineralization timescales</cite>. These system-specific controls imply that forecasts of terrestrial carbon loss through leached DOC must resolve catchment composition, riverine transport, estuarine photochemical and microbial processing, and coastal redox/hydrodynamic sorting.

Implications for estimating terrestrial carbon loss
- Rivers as conduits, not simple reactors. <cite id="ee65992e-2">Rivers annually transport ~0.25 Gt of DOC to the ocean, but the fraction mineralized before export depends on DOM quality and processing within each catchment, estuary, and coastal zone</cite>. <cite id="9ea9bbc4-0">Photomineralization can dominate water-column DOC processing in high-latitude rivers and margins, converting DOC to DIC without net export to the deep ocean</cite>. Conversely, <cite id="9ea9bbc4-1">in temperate estuaries like the Tyne, photochemical losses may amount to only a small fraction of annual DOC inputs, implying that a larger terrestrial DOC fraction survives to be delivered to the coastal ocean</cite>. Thus, terrestrial carbon loss is path-dependent and cannot be reduced to a single, uniform kinetic constant applied across catchments.

Practical synthesis
- Leached DOC is a mixture of reactive classes whose mineralization kinetics depend on molecular properties (aromaticity, molecular weight, chromophoric “lability”), microbial energetics (BGE, nutrients, light, temperature), and photochemical processing. <cite id="187ac718-0">Autochthonous vs. allochthonous contrasts in chemistry imply different initial labilities</cite> <cite id="ee65992e-2">DOM quality explains up to ~75% of bacterial growth variability and inversely relates to BGE via stoichiometry and environment</cite> <cite id="ee65992e-3">and sunlight can accelerate mineralization by ~5× in many inland waters</cite>. Therefore, kinetics are not uniform across aquatic systems.

- Predictability is feasible at a local scale when DOM composition and environmental context are known. <cite id="ee65992e-2">If DOM quality (e.g., absorbance/fluorescence, DOC: DON) and environmental variables are measured, bacterial growth and BGE can be forecast, enabling parameterization of first-order mineralization</cite>. <cite id="9ea9bbc4-0">Optical proxies of lability and photomineralization can predict both direct DIC formation and enhanced biomineralization, improving carbon-loss estimates</cite>. However, cross-system extrapolation fails without accounting for: (i) catchment-driven changes in DOM quality, (ii) light exposure and photochemical alteration during transport, (iii) estuarine mixing and redox, and (iv) seasonal and hydrologic modulation. <cite id="ee65992e-2">Land-use changes alter DOM quality and hence bacterial processing</cite> <cite id="ee65992e-3">and predicting reactivity remains challenging across diverse inland waters</cite> <cite id="187ac718-2">salinity/hydrology gradients in wetlands and estuaries further break predictability</cite>.

Bottom line
Leached DOC does not follow uniform mineralization kinetics; rather, it comprises heterogeneous, chemically and optically distinct classes whose rates diverge with composition, light, nutrients, temperature, and redox. <cite id="ee65992e-0">DOM components have different fates along rivers to ocean</cite> <cite id="187ac718-0">allochthonous DOM is generally less bioavailable than autochthonous</cite> <cite id="ee65992e-3">and photomineralization can dominate CO2 production in many systems</cite>. While terrestrial carbon loss can be predicted locally if DOM “size-class” lability and environmental drivers are resolved, generalizing across systems without these constraints is unreliable; hence, “leaked” DOC is predictable as a carbon loss only when kinetics are parameterized for each catchment–estuary–coastal context. <cite id="ee65992e-2">Predictions that ignore DOM quality and environmental controls are likely to be inaccurate</cite> <cite id="ee65992e-3">and empirical work shows predicting DOC reactivity has been challenging</cite>. Title: Biogeochemical and Physical Controls on the Microbial Degradation of Dissolved Organic Matter Along a Temperate Microtidal Estuary
Snippet: Estuaries are "hotspots" of organic matter (OM) cycling and play an important role in the coastal carbon cycle due to their position at the land-sea interface (McClain et al. 2003). This location is characterized by both allochthonous (i.e., produced outside the estuary) inputs of OM from rivers and the surrounding catchments and autochthonous (i.e., produced within the estuary) inputs of OM from primary and secondary production. During transport to the coastal ocean, allochthonous and autochthonous sources of OM may be modified and removed by processes such as flocculation, sinking, photolysis, and microbial degradation (Canuel and Hardison 2016;Bianchi 2007 and references therein;Hedges and Keil 1999). Understanding the effect of these processes on OM is important for determining the trophic status of estuaries, developing coastal carbon budgets, and assessing the role of estuaries as either sources or sinks of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) (Borges and Abril 2011;Cai 2011). 

Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) comprises most of the total dissolved organic matter (DOM) pool, but DOM also includes other constituents such as dissolved organic nitrogen (DON), dissolved organic phosphorus (DOP), and dissolved organic sulfur (DOS) (Bianchi 2007 and references therein). In addition, chromophoric dissolved organic matter (CDOM) is a component of DOM that absorbs light. Within CDOM, there is a fraction that fluoresces (i.e., fluorescent dissolved organic matter or fDOM). Optical properties (absorbance and fluorescence) of DOM are often used to identify the source and composition of DOM in estuaries and other aquatic ecosystems (Stedmon and Nelson 2015). DOC dynamics are often used to describe the entire DOM pool (Carlson and Hansell 2015), but DOM components may have different fates depending on the relative contributions of each to the total DOM pool (e.g., elemental stoichiometry) and their interactions with biotic and abiotic environmental factors (Graeber et al. 2021;Asmala et al. 2013;Lønberg et al. 2010).

Title: The relative importance of photodegradation and biodegradation of terrestrially derived dissolved organic carbon across four lakes of differing trophic status
Snippet: Estimates suggest that lakes respire about half of the annual 2 Gt flux of carbon to the oceans each year as CO 2 (Cole et al., 1994;Tranvik et al., 2009;Tranvik, 2014). The traditional paradigm has been that the dominant mechanism causing the release of excess CO 2 from lakes is the bacterial respiration of DOC (biodegradation), with photomineralization (conversion of DOC to CO 2 ) accounting for only 10 % of bacterial rates (Granéli et al., 1996;del Giorgio et al., 1997;Jonsson et al., 2001). However, research on over 200 Arctic lakes, rivers, and streams revealed that sunlight dominated the processing of DOC, and photomineralization rates were, on average, 5× greater than dark bacterial respiration rates (Cory et al., 2014). In addition, the source of inland water CO 2 remains uncertain, due in large part to a lack of measurements (Raymond et al., 2013;Lapierre et al., 2013;Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015), and predicting DOC reactivity has been challenging (Evans et al., 2017). Quantifying the dominant degradation pathways for terrestrial DOC from a range of lakes will improve estimates of carbon fluxes, particularly for mineralization rates that currently have a high degree of uncertainty (Hanson et al., 2014). 

Many past studies have focused on testing the effects of photodegradation and biodegradation on DOC quantity individually, but they have not simultaneously evaluated how these two processes alter the colored dissolved organic carbon (CDOM; Granéli et al., 1996;Koehler et al., 2014;Vachon et al., 2016a). CDOM is the fraction of dissolved organic matter that is capable of absorbing light. The effects of sunlight on DOC are not isolated to only increasing mineralization rates. Photodegradation can also decrease the color and molecular weight of DOC, which can increase light availability and the subsequent bacterial respiration of DOC (Bertilsson and Tranvik, 2000;Amado et al., 2003;Chen and Jaffé, 2016).

Title: High bacterial carbon demand and low growth efficiency at a tropical hypereutrophic estuary: importance of dissolved organic matter remineralization
Snippet: Bacterioplankton play multiple roles in aquatic systems, converting high amounts of allochthonous and autochthonous organic material into nutrients (organic remineralization) and biomass (organic production). Understanding the extent and the regulating factors of each of these bacterial metabolic pathways is thus imperative to comprehend the carbon cycle in those systems. The amount of carbon incorporated by bacterioplankton is partitioned into growth (anabolism) and maintenance processes (catabolism). The bacterial carbon demand (BCD) is thus the sum of biomass produced (=bacterial production: BP) and the energetic loss (=bacterial respiration: BR). The efficiency to which the carbon incorporated is converted into biomass, i.e., the bacterial growth efficiency (BGE) is thus estimated as BP/BCD (DEL GIORGIO; COLE, 1998). 

Bacterial carbon consumption has been usually derived from bacterial production rates assuming constant growth efficiencies (GASOL et al., 2008). Nevertheless, several studies showed a great spatial and temporal variability in BGE within and among systems, due to several abiotic and biotic factors like temperature, inorganic nutrients availability, dissolved organic matter (DOM) quality, light incidence and grazing pressure (APPLE; DEL GIORGIO, 2007;APPLE et al., 2006;ASMALA et al., 2014;BERGGREN et al., 2010;CORY et al., 2010;RAM et al., 2003). The need for simultaneous in situ estimates of bacterial production and respiration rates became thus imperative to accurately evaluate the bacterial carbon metabolism in the aquatic systems and understand its regulation. 

Estuarine systems are increasingly subject to eutrophication processes due to the rapid population growth and consequent density increase along the coast (DAY et al., 2013). The high and continuous input of allochthonous nutrients and organic material from the surrounding lands and the domestic sewage leads to high phytoplankton and bacterial growth (BARRERA-ALBA et al., 2008;GAULKE et al., 2010;GUENTHER;VALENTIN, 2008b;MORTAZAVI et al.;2012;SCHUMANN et al., 2003;YUAN et al., 2010).

The high and continuous input of allochthonous nutrients and organic material from the surrounding lands and the domestic sewage leads to high phytoplankton and bacterial growth (BARRERA-ALBA et al., 2008;GAULKE et al., 2010;GUENTHER;VALENTIN, 2008b;MORTAZAVI et al.;2012;SCHUMANN et al., 2003;YUAN et al., 2010).

documents.title: Biogeochemical and Physical Controls on the Microbial Degradation of Dissolved Organic Matter Along a Temperate Microtidal Estuary
documents.snippet:
Estuaries are "hotspots" of organic matter (OM) cycling and play an important role in the coastal carbon cycle due to their position at the land-sea interface (McClain et al. 2003). This location is characterized by both allochthonous (i.e., produced outside the estuary) inputs of OM from rivers and the surrounding catchments and autochthonous (i.e., produced within the estuary) inputs of OM from primary and secondary production. During transport to the coastal ocean, allochthonous and autochthonous sources of OM may be modified and removed by processes such as flocculation, sinking, photolysis, and microbial degradation (Canuel and Hardison 2016;Bianchi 2007 and references therein;Hedges and Keil 1999). Understanding the effect of these processes on OM is important for determining the trophic status of estuaries, developing coastal carbon budgets, and assessing the role of estuaries as either sources or sinks of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) (Borges and Abril 2011;Cai 2011). 

Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) comprises most of the total dissolved organic matter (DOM) pool, but DOM also includes other constituents such as dissolved organic nitrogen (DON), dissolved organic phosphorus (DOP), and dissolved organic sulfur (DOS) (Bianchi 2007 and references therein). In addition, chromophoric dissolved organic matter (CDOM) is a component of DOM that absorbs light. Within CDOM, there is a fraction that fluoresces (i.e., fluorescent dissolved organic matter or fDOM). Optical properties (absorbance and fluorescence) of DOM are often used to identify the source and composition of DOM in estuaries and other aquatic ecosystems (Stedmon and Nelson 2015). DOC dynamics are often used to describe the entire DOM pool (Carlson and Hansell 2015), but DOM components may have different fates depending on the relative contributions of each to the total DOM pool (e.g., elemental stoichiometry) and their interactions with biotic and abiotic environmental factors (Graeber et al. 2021;Asmala et al. 2013;Lønberg et al. 2010).

documents.title: Leaching of carbon from native and non-native leaf litter of subtropical riparian forests
documents.snippet: Our study considered only one stage of the decomposition process (leaching). The leaching of soluble compounds is the first step in the process of decomposition of allochthonous organic matter in streams. This step is important for the release of soluble compounds (e.g., phenols), which may influence microbial colonization and subsequent fragmentation. In addition, the dissolved fractions of carbon are fundamental for the direct incorporation by aquatic plants and microorganisms. In addition, the results presented in this paper reinforce the need for a more careful look at ecological processes. Integrated ecosystem assessment, considering both the structural and functional aspects, as well as physical, chemical, and biological factors would lead to a more complete assessment of the actual environmental conditions of habitats.

documents.title: Bioavailability of riverine dissolved organic matter in three Baltic Sea estuaries and the effect of catchment land use
documents.snippet:
Organic matter consists of particulate and dissolved phases (POM and DOM), which are traditionally separated on the rather arbitrary criteria of filter pore sizes typically ranging between 0.1 and 0.7 µm. POM and DOM in aquatic systems are either derived from organisms within the system (autochthonous) or transported into the system via rivers and atmospheric deposition (allochthonous). The DOM pool is vital for the functioning of food webs in aquatic systems since it forms the basis for heterotrophic activity and its breakdown is central to the regeneration of inorganic nutrients (Hansell and Carlsson, 2002;Søndergaard and Thomas, 2004).

Rivers and estuaries link terrestrial systems and the oceans, and rivers are a major source of allochthonous carbon to the global ocean, transporting an estimated 0.25 Gt of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) annually (Hedges et al., 1997;Jiao et al., 2010). Nitrogen fluxes from terrestrial systems to aquatic systems generally increase with greater degree of anthropogenic disturbance to a catchment (Stedmon et al., 2006), and presently anthropogenically induced fluxes of nitrogen exceed natural fluxes globally (Vitousek et al., 1997). These fluxes of both organic carbon and nitrogen are essential to the overall productivity of estuarine ecosystems since they are the basis of the heterotrophic food webs (Mann, 1988).

Variation in DOM quality can explain up to 75 % of the variability of bacterial growth in estuarine waters (Hopkinson et al., 1998). Bacterial growth efficiency (BGE) describes the proportion of carbon that heterotrophic bacterial cells transfer from substrate (DOM) to biomass (del Giorgio and Cole, 1998) and can be used as a metric to characterize bacterial DOM utilization. The quantity of DOM, as a substrate for heterotrophs, has been shown to affect BGE only at very low concentrations (Eiler et al., 2003), whereas the quality of DOM has a stronger influence on BGE, e.g., the DOC : DON (dissolved organic nitrogen) ratio is typically inversely proportional to BGE (Kroer, 1993). documents.title: The relative importance of photodegradation and biodegradation of terrestrially derived dissolved organic carbon across four lakes of differing trophic status
documents.snippet:
Estimates suggest that lakes respire about half of the annual 2 Gt flux of carbon to the oceans each year as CO 2 (Cole et al., 1994;Tranvik et al., 2009;Tranvik, 2014). The traditional paradigm has been that the dominant mechanism causing the release of excess CO 2 from lakes is the bacterial respiration of DOC (biodegradation), with photomineralization (conversion of DOC to CO 2 ) accounting for only 10 % of bacterial rates (Granéli et al., 1996;del Giorgio et al., 1997;Jonsson et al., 2001). However, research on over 200 Arctic lakes, rivers, and streams revealed that sunlight dominated the processing of DOC, and photomineralization rates were, on average, 5× greater than dark bacterial respiration rates (Cory et al., 2014). In addition, the source of inland water CO 2 remains uncertain, due in large part to a lack of measurements (Raymond et al., 2013;Lapierre et al., 2013;Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015), and predicting DOC reactivity has been challenging (Evans et al., 2017). Quantifying the dominant degradation pathways for terrestrial DOC from a range of lakes will improve estimates of carbon fluxes, particularly for mineralization rates that currently have a high degree of uncertainty (Hanson et al., 2014). 

Many past studies have focused on testing the effects of photodegradation and biodegradation on DOC quantity individually, but they have not simultaneously evaluated how these two processes alter the colored dissolved organic carbon (CDOM; Granéli et al., 1996;Koehler et al., 2014;Vachon et al., 2016a). CDOM is the fraction of dissolved organic matter that is capable of absorbing light. The effects of sunlight on DOC are not isolated to only increasing mineralization rates. Photodegradation can also decrease the color and molecular weight of DOC, which can increase light availability and the subsequent bacterial respiration of DOC (Bertilsson and Tranvik, 2000;Amado et al., 2003;Chen and Jaffé, 2016).

documents.title: High bacterial carbon demand and low growth efficiency at a tropical hypereutrophic estuary: importance of dissolved organic matter remineralization
documents.snippet:
Bacterioplankton play multiple roles in aquatic systems, converting high amounts of allochthonous and autochthonous organic material into nutrients (organic remineralization) and biomass (organic production). Understanding the extent and the regulating factors of each of these bacterial metabolic pathways is thus imperative to comprehend the carbon cycle in those systems. The amount of carbon incorporated by bacterioplankton is partitioned into growth (anabolism) and maintenance processes (catabolism). The bacterial carbon demand (BCD) is thus the sum of biomass produced (=bacterial production: BP) and the energetic loss (=bacterial respiration: BR). The efficiency to which the carbon incorporated is converted into biomass, i.e., the bacterial growth efficiency (BGE) is thus estimated as BP/BCD (DEL GIORGIO; COLE, 1998). 

Bacterial carbon consumption has been usually derived from bacterial production rates assuming constant growth efficiencies (GASOL et al., 2008). Nevertheless, several studies showed a great spatial and temporal variability in BGE within and among systems, due to several abiotic and biotic factors like temperature, inorganic nutrients availability, dissolved organic matter (DOM) quality, light incidence and grazing pressure (APPLE; DEL GIORGIO, 2007;APPLE et al., 2006;ASMALA et al., 2014;BERGGREN et al., 2010;CORY et al., 2010;RAM et al., 2003). The need for simultaneous in situ estimates of bacterial production and respiration rates became thus imperative to accurately evaluate the bacterial carbon metabolism in the aquatic systems and understand its regulation.

Title: Organic matter cycling in a model restored wetland receiving complex effluent
Snippet: Yet for dissolved organic matter (DOM), net processing (production versus consumption) can vary with the source and composition of DOM inputs, as well as wetland conditions (vegetation type, hydrology, soil type, temperature, and pH, etc.), as shown for both constructed and natural wetlands in the U.S. (Lu et al. 2003;Pinney et al. 2000). Studies from around the world from natural and experimental systems have shown that the net outcome of DOM cycling also depends on processes including microbial mineralization and photodegradation of DOM (Hertkorn et al. 2016;Li et al. 2008;Stottmeister et al. 2003). Further, anaerobic conditions in wetland sediments can restrict the efficiency of DOM mineralization, but can also enhance removal through processes such as denitrification (Kayranli et al. 2010;Werker et al. 2002), sedimentation, and sorption (Fisher and Acreman 2004;Vymazal 2007). Taken together, wetland restoration is a potential mechanism to improve water quality through increased inorganic nutrient processing (Cheng et al. 2020), yet the role of wetlands, especially treatment wetlands, in net OM cycling and remediation is not clear. 

Overall, DOM represents a complex mixture of organic molecules including macro-and micro-nutrients that support both auto-and heterotrophic activities, which can influence physical and chemical properties in aquatic ecosystems (Findlay and Sinsabaugh 2003). Broadly-speaking, DOM is categorized into two types: autochthonous (internally-generated in an ecosystem) and allochthonous (externally-derived) DOM. Internally-derived, autochthonous DOM is generally less aromatic (more aliphatic), with lower molecular weight (LMW) and greater bioavailability (Findlay and Sinsabaugh 2003). Natural allochthonous DOM (e.g., from terrestrial soils and forests) is transported into aquatic ecosystems and contains more aromatic, complex compounds (high molecular weight DOM, HMW) with higher C to N ratios, that tend to be less bioavailable (Findlay and Sinsabaugh 2003;van den Berg et al. 2012).

Title: Assessing coastal carbon variability in two Delaware tidal marshes
Snippet: Carbon density, organic matter concentration, and dry bulk density were significantly different between the St. Jones and Blackbird Creek Reserves, suggesting that there were different carbon storage quantities between these two tidal wetlands. While we do note more core samples were taken at St. Jones Reserve (n = 42) as compared to the Blackbird  Blackbird Creek Reserve is a tidal freshwater marsh (oligohaline) with a mean salinity of 1.9 ± 2.1 ppt, while the St. Jones Reserve is a more mesohaline saltmarsh with a mean salinity of 10.8 ± 6.9 ppt. The finding of lower carbon density values at the Blackbird Creek Reserve was unexpected as higher saline waters generally allow for more sulfate reduction, which can turnover organic matter at a faster rate compared to metabolic pathways such as methanogenesis (Sutton-Grier et al. 2011;Weston et al. 2006). For example, soil organic carbon concentrations were nearly 4.5 times greater in a tidal freshwater marsh compared to a saltmarsh in the Scheldt Estuary (Van De Broek et al. 2016). In this European study, regions of the estuary with reduced salinity exhibited higher rates of carbon burial and the depositing allochthonous terrestrial matter was a more stable carbon form. 

In general, most tidal wetland studies have shown that soil organic carbon stocks typically decrease with an increasing salinity (Baustian et al. 2017;Christopher Craft 2007;Hansen et al. 2017). A previous tidal wetland study in Delaware found a greater carbon stock in tidal freshwater wetlands compared to oligohaline and mesohaline systems (Weston et al. 2014). Low salinity tidal marshes have demonstrated suppressed decomposition, likely due to limitations in the availability of sulfate and reduced rate of root decomposition (Craft 2007). In the current study, the higher carbon stocks at the St. Jones Reserve could be due to several contributing factors, including differences in sediment accumulation rates, organic matter decomposition rates, and the stability of the organic matter.

Title: Factors Regulating the Potential for Freshwater Mineral Soil Wetlands to Function as Natural Climate Solutions
Snippet: Autochthonous organic matter production under aerobic conditions and accumulation under anaerobic conditions are the main pathways for carbon accumulation in peatlands that are characterized by relatively high carbon content (e.g., > 65%; Ausseil et al. 2015). Meanwhile, allochthonous dissolved and particulate organic matter from upstream catchments as well as autochthonous organic matter production under anaerobic environmental conditions are considered the main sources for carbon accumulation in mineral soil wetlands (Bridgham et al. 2006;Loder and Finkelstein 2020). Resulting from allochthonous dissolved material inputs, nutrient levels and plant productivity are usually high in mineral soil wetlands (Ausseil et al. 2015). Yet, mineral soil wetlands store less organic matter compared to peatlands since they are characterized by faster decomposition rate (Loder and Finkelstein 2020). Most mineral soil wetlands comprise mineral soil substrates, but some comprise > 50% organic soil substrates (Bridgham et al. 2006). 

Freshwater mineral soil wetlands are present in numerous large wetland complexes worldwide, such as the Prairie Pothole Region of North America (Bansal et al. 2023b), the Sanjiang Plain of Northeast China (Zhang et al. 2008), and the Florida Everglades (Mitsch and Gosselink 2015). Despite wetlands typically having less carbon stored in their soils as compared to peatlands, they play important roles in regional carbon storage due to their extensive areal extent (e.g., freshwater mineral soil wetlands comprise 95% of the total wetland area in the USA) (Nahlik and Fennessy 2016). However, there is high uncertainty in the carbon sequestration potential and CO 2 and CH 4 flux mechanisms of wetlands and therefore their potential as NCS (Bridgham et al. 2006;Ausseil et al. 2015;Nahlik and Fennessy 2016;Loder and Finkelstein 2020;Villa et al. 2020;Creed et al. 2022). 

Hydrologically connected wetlands within an associated hydrological catchment are called wetlandscapes (Fig. 1) (Thorslund et al. 2017).

Title: Ecosystem Capacity for Microbial Biodegradation of Munitions Compounds and Phenanthrene in Three Coastal Waterways in North Carolina, United States
Snippet: Energetics Mineralization along the Newport River Estuary Transect. Substrate mineralization rates were measured by incubation of estuarine samples with 14 C-labeled substrates to evolve 14 CO 2 . Detectable TNT mineralization (Tmin) rates (>0.01 μg C L −1 day −1 ) in water column samples for the NPRE ranged from 0.14 (±0.05) to 0.45 (±0.17) μg C L −1 day −1 for the 14 Nov sampling (low antecedent precipitation (AP): 34 mm over previous 7 day), 0.14 (±0.03) to 0.51 (±0.03) μg C L −1 day −1 for the 15 Aug sampling (moderate AP: 102 mm), and 0.12 (±0.05) to 0.20 (±0.04) μg C L −1 day −1 for the 14 Aug sampling (high AP: 200 mm; Figure 1 and Table S1). These ranges for the low and moderate AP sampling were very similar to each other and slightly lower for the highest AP sampling. In general, Tmin rates were more rapid in the lower estuary (salinity >21; Figure 1A), as they were for phenanthrene mineralization (Pmin), as previously reported. 19 Heterotrophic bacterial production (BP) ranged from 7.0 (±1.0) at the highest salinity (15 Aug) to 159 (±13) μg C L −1 day −1 at the Cypress bog headwaters (14 Nov; Table S1 and Osburn et al. 19 ) for the three samplings of NPRE. Comparing min/BP can give an indication of the relative importance of carbon substrate metabolism to overall carbon demand by the assemblage. Tmin/BP generally increased with salinity and decreased with higher AP (Figure 1D). If dissolved organic carbon (DOC) associated with precipitation was preferentially metabolized by the estuarine assemblage, one would expect there to be lower contaminant min/BP ratios with higher AP.

Internally-derived, autochthonous DOM is generally less aromatic (more aliphatic), with lower molecular weight (LMW) and greater bioavailability (Findlay and Sinsabaugh 2003). Natural allochthonous DOM (e.g., from terrestrial soils and forests) is transported into aquatic ecosystems and contains more aromatic, complex compounds (high molecular weight DOM, HMW) with higher C to N ratios, that tend to be less bioavailable (Findlay and Sinsabaugh 2003;van den Berg et al. 2012).

documents.title: Biogeochemical and Physical Controls on the Microbial Degradation of Dissolved Organic Matter Along a Temperate Microtidal Estuary
documents.snippet:
Estuaries are "hotspots" of organic matter (OM) cycling and play an important role in the coastal carbon cycle due to their position at the land-sea interface (McClain et al. 2003). This location is characterized by both allochthonous (i.e., produced outside the estuary) inputs of OM from rivers and the surrounding catchments and autochthonous (i.e., produced within the estuary) inputs of OM from primary and secondary production. During transport to the coastal ocean, allochthonous and autochthonous sources of OM may be modified and removed by processes such as flocculation, sinking, photolysis, and microbial degradation (Canuel and Hardison 2016;Bianchi 2007 and references therein;Hedges and Keil 1999). Understanding the effect of these processes on OM is important for determining the trophic status of estuaries, developing coastal carbon budgets, and assessing the role of estuaries as either sources or sinks of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) (Borges and Abril 2011;Cai 2011). 

Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) comprises most of the total dissolved organic matter (DOM) pool, but DOM also includes other constituents such as dissolved organic nitrogen (DON), dissolved organic phosphorus (DOP), and dissolved organic sulfur (DOS) (Bianchi 2007 and references therein). In addition, chromophoric dissolved organic matter (CDOM) is a component of DOM that absorbs light. Within CDOM, there is a fraction that fluoresces (i.e., fluorescent dissolved organic matter or fDOM). Optical properties (absorbance and fluorescence) of DOM are often used to identify the source and composition of DOM in estuaries and other aquatic ecosystems (Stedmon and Nelson 2015). DOC dynamics are often used to describe the entire DOM pool (Carlson and Hansell 2015), but DOM components may have different fates depending on the relative contributions of each to the total DOM pool (e.g., elemental stoichiometry) and their interactions with biotic and abiotic environmental factors (Graeber et al. 2021;Asmala et al. 2013;Lønberg et al. 2010).

documents.title: Assessing coastal carbon variability in two Delaware tidal marshes
documents.snippet:
Carbon density, organic matter concentration, and dry bulk density were significantly different between the St. Jones and Blackbird Creek Reserves, suggesting that there were different carbon storage quantities between these two tidal wetlands. While we do note more core samples were taken at St. Jones Reserve (n = 42) as compared to the Blackbird  Blackbird Creek Reserve is a tidal freshwater marsh (oligohaline) with a mean salinity of 1.9 ± 2.1 ppt, while the St. Jones Reserve is a more mesohaline saltmarsh with a mean salinity of 10.8 ± 6.9 ppt. The finding of lower carbon density values at the Blackbird Creek Reserve was unexpected as higher saline waters generally allow for more sulfate reduction, which can turnover organic matter at a faster rate compared to metabolic pathways such as methanogenesis (Sutton-Grier et al. 2011;Weston et al. 2006). For example, soil organic carbon concentrations were nearly 4.5 times greater in a tidal freshwater marsh compared to a saltmarsh in the Scheldt Estuary (Van De Broek et al. 2016). In this European study, regions of the estuary with reduced salinity exhibited higher rates of carbon burial and the depositing allochthonous terrestrial matter was a more stable carbon form. 

In general, most tidal wetland studies have shown that soil organic carbon stocks typically decrease with an increasing salinity (Baustian et al. 2017;Christopher Craft 2007;Hansen et al. 2017). A previous tidal wetland study in Delaware found a greater carbon stock in tidal freshwater wetlands compared to oligohaline and mesohaline systems (Weston et al. 2014). Low salinity tidal marshes have demonstrated suppressed decomposition, likely due to limitations in the availability of sulfate and reduced rate of root decomposition (Craft 2007). In the current study, the higher carbon stocks at the St. Jones Reserve could be due to several contributing factors, including differences in sediment accumulation rates, organic matter decomposition rates, and the stability of the organic matter.

documents.title: Factors Regulating the Potential for Freshwater Mineral Soil Wetlands to Function as Natural Climate Solutions
documents.snippet:
Autochthonous organic matter production under aerobic conditions and accumulation under anaerobic conditions are the main pathways for carbon accumulation in peatlands that are characterized by relatively high carbon content (e.g., > 65%; Ausseil et al. 2015). Meanwhile, allochthonous dissolved and particulate organic matter from upstream catchments as well as autochthonous organic matter production under anaerobic environmental conditions are considered the main sources for carbon accumulation in mineral soil wetlands (Bridgham et al. 2006;Loder and Finkelstein 2020). Resulting from allochthonous dissolved material inputs, nutrient levels and plant productivity are usually high in mineral soil wetlands (Ausseil et al. 2015). Yet, mineral soil wetlands store less organic matter compared to peatlands since they are characterized by faster decomposition rate (Loder and Finkelstein 2020). Most mineral soil wetlands comprise mineral soil substrates, but some comprise > 50% organic soil substrates (Bridgham et al. 2006). 

Freshwater mineral soil wetlands are present in numerous large wetland complexes worldwide, such as the Prairie Pothole Region of North America (Bansal et al. 2023b), the Sanjiang Plain of Northeast China (Zhang et al. 2008), and the Florida Everglades (Mitsch and Gosselink 2015). Despite wetlands typically having less carbon stored in their soils as compared to peatlands, they play important roles in regional carbon storage due to their extensive areal extent (e.g., freshwater mineral soil wetlands comprise 95% of the total wetland area in the USA) (Nahlik and Fennessy 2016). However, there is high uncertainty in the carbon sequestration potential and CO 2 and CH 4 flux mechanisms of wetlands and therefore their potential as NCS (Bridgham et al. 2006;Ausseil et al. 2015;Nahlik and Fennessy 2016;Loder and Finkelstein 2020;Villa et al. 2020;Creed et al. 2022). 

Hydrologically connected wetlands within an associated hydrological catchment are called wetlandscapes (Fig. 1) (Thorslund et al. 2017).

documents.snippet: Energetics Mineralization along the Newport River Estuary Transect. Substrate mineralization rates were measured by incubation of estuarine samples with 14 C-labeled substrates to evolve 14 CO 2 . If dissolved organic carbon (DOC) associated with precipitation was preferentially metabolized by the estuarine assemblage, one would expect there to be lower contaminant min/BP ratios with higher AP.

Title: Photomineralization of organic carbon in a eutrophic, semiarid estuary
Snippet: Past studies showed that photomineralization of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in the aquatic environment is a major removal mechanism for terrestrially derived DOC (Miller and Zepp 1995;Hernes and Benner 2003;Aarnos et al. 2018). For example, at least 15% of Rio Negro (a tributary of the Amazon River) DOC is photoreactive after sunlight exposure for 27 h, and the photomineralization rate of DOC ($4.0 μM hr −1 ) is approximately sevenfold greater than that of bacterial DOC utilization in Rio Negro surface waters (Amon and Benner 1996). Similarly, Congo River DOC is also shown to be highly photoactive, with over 95% decrease in lignin phenol concentration after a $38-day natural sunlight exposure equivalence (Spencer et al. 2009). Overall, photomineralization of DOC accounts for 70-90% of total DOC processed in the water column of Arctic lakes and rivers (Cory et al. 2014). Photomineralization that converts DOC into dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) is also an important sink for organic carbon (OC) in both coastal and open ocean environments (Vodacek et al. 1997;Tracy and Sybil 2001;Brinkmann et al. 2003;Nieto-Cid et al. 2006;Stubbins et al. 2006;Wang et al. 2009;Xie et al. 2009;White et al. 2010;Stubbins et al. 2011;Reader and Miller 2012;Fichot and Benner 2014). In addition to photodegradation induced direct mineralization, Fichot and Benner (2014) reported that photomineralization can significantly enhance biomineralization ($50%) in the mixed layer in a large river-influenced ocean margin in the northern Gulf of Mexico. 

Past studies have shown that DOC of different origins may have different photoreactivities. For example, Opsahl and Benner (1998) reported rapid photochemical degradation of terrestrially derived lignin phenols in seawater. This finding was supported by the changes in DOC stable carbon isotopic composition before and after photochemical alterations of soil solutions, river water, and estuarine water.

Title: Carbon monoxide apparent quantum yields and photoproduction in the Tyne estuary
Snippet: A first order estimate of total dissolved organic carbon (DOC) photomineralization in the Tyne estuary was made by extrapolating from CO photoproduction using a ratio of dissolved inorganic carbon:biolabile DOC:CO photoproduction of 20:13:1 (Miller and Zepp, 1995;Gao and Zepp, 1998;Miller et al., 2002). Estimated production of dissolved inorganic carbon, mineralization through photoproduction of biolabile carbon and total DOC mineralization were thus 20-71, 13-46 and 33-117 Tonnes-C yr −1 , respectively. Riverine DOC inputs to the Tyne estuary were estimated at ∼25 600 Tonnes-C yr −1 based upon an annually averaged freshwater flow rate of 55 m 3 s −1 for the period 1998-2001 (Environment Agency, UK; http://www. environment-agency.gov.uk) and an annually averaged freshwater DOC concentration of 1230 µM (Spencer et al., 2007). Using these values, estimated DOC removal through CO photoproduction amounts to a modest 0.004-0.014% of total DOC inputs and total photochemical losses of DOC within the estuary are similarly small: 0.13-0.46% of the DOC input.

Title: Photomineralization of organic carbon in a eutrophic, semiarid estuary
Snippet: The effect of photomineralization on the carbon cycle in a eutrophic, semiarid estuary (Baffin Bay, Texas) was investigated using closed‐system incubations. Photochemical production rate of dissolved inorganic carbon ranged from 0.16 to 0.68 μM hr−1, with a daily removal of 0.3∼1.5% of the standing stock of dissolved organic carbon (DOC). The photomineralization rate was negatively correlated with chlorophyll a concentration, suggesting that plankton‐derived DOC was less photoreactive to solar radiation. The stable carbon isotope composition (δ13C∼ −18.6‰) of degraded DOC, as calculated using the DIC “Keeling” plot, further indicated high photochemical lability of 13C‐enriched DOC in this semiarid environment. Our finding showed that photomineralization of 13C‐enriched DOC is an important component of carbon cycle in this system, and this process does not necessarily remove 13C‐depleted organic carbon as observed in other coastal systems.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer explicitly rejects the uniformity premise in multiple places: the opening summary states DOC 'does not follow uniform mineralization kinetics across aquatic systems,' and the conclusion affirms 'Leached DOC does not follow uniform mineralization kinetics.' It provides extensive evidence of kinetic variability across system types, including: (1) photomineralization dominating in Arctic lakes/rivers at 5× bacterial respiration rates, (2) contrasting photochemical losses between systems (0.004-0.014% in Tyne estuary vs. 0.3-1.5% daily in Baffin Bay), (3) redox-driven differences in coastal/wetland systems, and (4) estuarine mixing effects. The answer concludes that this variability makes leaching NOT predictable without system-specific context, stating 'forecasts of terrestrial carbon loss through leached DOC must resolve catchment composition, riverine transport, estuarine photochemical and microbial processing, and coastal redox/hydrodynamic sorting' and that 'generalizing across systems without these constraints is unreliable.'

attempts.answer:
Overview and definitions
Lysimeters directly sample soil solution or near‐subsurface water at discrete points and depths, often via zero‐tension or suction devices, and quantify dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in filtered water for export budgeting; stream gauges monitor discharge continuously and integrate periodic water‐quality samples to estimate loads, typically assuming conservative mixing of DOC in stormflow and baseflow <cite id="ccb53b9c-3">Zero-tension lysimeters allow for gauging the flux of metals associated with rainfall infiltration. They provide useful information to assess ecosystem input and output budgets</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-0">In 1988, 39 zero-tension lysimeters per watershed at 15 sites within each watershed were installed to monitor soil solution volume and chemistry at the bottom of each soil horizon: A, B, and C when possible</cite><cite id="3348319a-4">At each of the catchments, discharge was recorded continuously and resampled to daily intervals, using 90° or 120° V-notch or H-flume sharp crested recording weirs and stage-discharge relationships from stilling walls and water-level recorders</cite><cite id="3348319a-4">Daily DOC loads (kg DOC ha−1 d−1) from each watershed were determined from daily measured discharge data and estimates of linearly interpolated DOC concentration data from approximately weekly DOC concentration measurements for each stream</cite>. Conceptually, lysimeter “soil water” TOC is often treated as DOC because particulate organic carbon is minor in boreal surface waters, making lysimeter TOC comparable to stream DOC concentrations in adjacent reaches <cite id="c6ceb1ac-1">It should be noted that suction lysimeters filter out particles of diameters larger than 1 µm. It has also been shown that boreal surface waters usually carry negligible amounts of particulate organic carbon (POC), making dissolved organic carbon (DOC) the dominant fraction (∼95%) of TOC</cite><cite id="c6ceb1ac-1">Consequently, the riparian soil water TOC concentrations presented in this study are directly comparable to dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations in the adjacent streams</cite>.

Do lysimeter and stream‐gauge DOC fluxes converge?
At fine scales and within seasons, the two approaches can align because lysimeter DOC targets the same dissolved pool that streams export, especially in systems with low particulate loadings; riparian soils can dominate stream DOC loads despite small areal footprint, which implies that well‐placed lysimeters in source zones can match integrated exports when those zones control loading <cite id="c6ceb1ac-1">Consequently, the riparian soil water TOC concentrations presented in this study are directly comparable to dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations in the adjacent streams</cite><cite id="3348319a-0">Dosskey and Bertsch found that riparian soil contributed over 90% of DOC flux in a stream, even though they covered only 6% of the catchment area</cite>. However, flux convergence is not guaranteed because the two methods integrate different hydrologic pathways and timeframes: lysimeters sample specific soil layers and flow components (vadose and shallow groundwater) while stream gauges integrate all runoff pathways over discharge that varies in residence time and mixing history <cite id="ccb53b9c-0">The water collected from the lysimeters represents the water and nutrients to which plants have direct access</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-2">Spatiotemporal Heterogeneity of Water Flowpaths Controls Dissolved Organic Carbon Sourcing in a Snow-Dominated, Headwater Catchment</cite>. Differences in concentration–discharge scaling and flowpath dominance are evident: lysimeter/soil‐solution and hillslope sample slopes differ from stream‐water low‐metal line mixing water line (LMWL) relationships, indicating that export behavior and dilution vary with discharge and source composition <cite id="ccb53b9c-2">.18) or lysimeter (p = 0.10) regression slopes, but differs from the LMWL and stream water slopes (p = 0.047, 0.037, respectively)</cite>. Seasonality reinforces divergence: spring freshet often dominates annual runoff and loads, with high discharge but lower in‐stream DOC concentrations, whereas summer/autumn show higher DOC concentrations and intermittent high loads from storm events, creating mismatch between steady, lysimeter‐based outputs and event‐integrated stream loads <cite id="3348319a-4">The spring freshet dominated annual runoff and loads at each site, while a combination of baseflow conditions and biogeochemical dormancy (low stream DOC concentrations and low discharge) resulted in lower winter loads at each site. Summer and autumn had higher in-stream DOC concentrations and lower discharge than peak spring discharge, instead responding to individual storm events</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-1">Rewetting through rain and storm events seems to play an important role on the release of carbon. During these events quick discharge components such as surface and sub-surface runoff rapidly transport C laterally, reducing time for microbiological degradation in the upper soil horizons and releasing dissolved organic matter into stream water</cite>.

Mechanisms for nonconvergence and representativeness
Several mechanisms drive divergence even when the exported solute is DOC. First, hydrologic separation means lysimeters footprint specific landscape positions (e.g., A, B, C horizons) while streams integrate upslope and riparian contributions, with riparian soils often responsible for the majority of DOC export despite small area, so a mismatch emerges if lysimeters underrepresent source zones <cite id="ccb53b9c-0">The water collected from the lysimeters represents the water and nutrients to which plants have direct access</cite><cite id="3348319a-0">Riparian soil contributed over 90% of DOC flux in a stream, even though they covered only 6% of the catchment area</cite>. Second, sampling vs. integration differences matter: lysimeter campaigns average two replicates per depth and interpolate time series to daily concentrations, whereas stream gauges integrate weekly to daily concentrations with continuous discharge; this leads to different weighting of storms, baseflow, and analytical method variations across sites <cite id="c6ceb1ac-3">Campaign concentrations were linearly interpolated in time (2008–2009) to obtain daily time series of DOC concentrations at each depth and site</cite><cite id="3348319a-4">Daily DOC loads were determined from daily discharge and interpolated concentrations from approximately weekly samples at each stream</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-4">Although there are some slight differences between methods between sites, comparisons of coherence are only being made between stream-pairs within each region, so that variations in DOC concentration due to method are not being directly compared</cite>. Third, event‐mean concentration (EMC) assumptions used to convert grab samples to loads can diverge from actual concentration–discharge behavior if dilution, sorption, or biodegradation change concentrations nonlinearly within events; lysimeters capture source variability across depths and seasons, while streams integrate mixed, often diluted, outputs <cite id="ccb53b9c-1">Results indicated a significant influence of discharge on DOC concentrations</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-2">DOC is highly variable at low flows and exhibits slight dilution at high flows</cite>. Finally, uncertainty in discharge measurements and cross‐sectional flow estimation propagates directly into load estimates, and spatial variability in soils and organic matter controls DOC export, further complicating convergence when upland and riparian zones differ in soil C pools and flow pathways <cite id="3348319a-1">One has to carefully consider the discharge data obtained with the handheld flow meter and the uncertainty introduced by the evaluation of the cross-section in the transformation of velocity data to volumes</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-1">A highly significant influence of organic soils on DOC concentrations was found. The dependency of DOC concentrations on organic soils has been already described by Aitkenhead et al. (1999). Dawson et al. (2008) concluded that the export rate of DOC depends on the carbon soil pool and therefore the organic fraction</cite>.

When do they converge?
Convergence is most likely when: (i) the catchment’s DOC export is dominated by a well‐characterized, representative source zone sampled by the lysimeter network (e.g., riparian soils), (ii) discharge and concentration series are aligned in time (continuous discharge with frequent concentration sampling), (iii) EMC assumptions are valid for the pollutant and event, and (iv) analytical methods and quality control are consistent across methods <cite id="ccb53b9c-0">The water collected from the lysimeters represents the water and nutrients to which plants have direct access</cite><cite id="3348319a-0">Riparian soil contributed over 90% of DOC flux in a stream, even though they covered only 6% of the catchment area</cite><cite id="3348319a-4">Daily DOC loads were determined from daily measured discharge data and estimates of linearly interpolated DOC concentration data from approximately weekly DOC concentration measurements for each stream</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-4">Although there are some slight differences between methods between sites, comparisons of coherence are only being made between stream-pairs within each region, so that variations in DOC concentration due to method are not being directly compared</cite>. Reconstructions that convert lysimeter campaign means into daily concentration profiles and compare to stream discharge demonstrate seasonal coherence patterns, indicating that integration over similar hydrologic regimes can make fluxes comparable at a temporal scale (e.g., spring freshet dominance) <cite id="c6ceb1ac-3">Campaign concentrations were linearly interpolated in time to obtain daily time series of DOC concentrations at each depth and site</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-3">Daily DOC loads from each watershed were determined from daily discharge and linearly interpolated concentrations from approximately weekly samples</cite><cite id="3348319a-4">Spring freshet dominated annual runoff and loads at each site, while a combination of baseflow conditions and biogeochemical dormancy resulted in lower winter loads</cite>. Conceptually, where particulate losses are negligible, soil water TOC and stream DOC are measuring the same dissolved pool, strengthening convergence expectations under matched scales and transport assumptions <cite id="c6ceb1ac-1">Boreal surface waters usually carry negligible amounts of particulate organic carbon, making dissolved organic carbon the dominant fraction</cite><cite id="c6ceb1ac-1">Riparian soil water TOC concentrations are directly comparable to DOC concentrations in the adjacent streams</cite>.

Which should carbon budgets trust?
For whole‐catchment budgets, a robust approach combines both: use stream gauges to integrate total export over time and space because they represent the basin outlet and all contributing flowpaths, while using lysimeters to resolve source zones and process controls and to diagnose budget components (e.g., riparian vs. upland contributions) and uncertainties <cite id="ccb53b9c-0">Stream discharge and precipitation have been monitored with stream chemistry samples taken since 1983</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-3">Zero-tension lysimeters allow for gauging the flux associated with rainfall infiltration. They provide useful information to assess ecosystem input and output budgets</cite><cite id="3348319a-0">Dissolved Organic Carbon in Headwater Streams and Riparian Soil Organic Carbon along an Altitudinal Gradient</cite>. In practice, stream‐integrated loads typically dominate annual carbon budgets and are easier to scale across watersheds, but they can miss fast, event‐driven fluxes or misattribute baseflow contributions if EMC assumptions are violated; lysimeters improve mechanistic fidelity in source zones but require careful placement and scaling to catchment area to avoid footprint bias <cite id="3348319a-4">Daily DOC loads from each watershed were determined from daily measured discharge data and estimates of linearly interpolated DOC concentration data from approximately weekly DOC concentration measurements for each stream</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-0">Lysimeters located to best represent the watershed as a whole</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-1">Rewetting through rain and storm events seems to play an important role on the release of carbon</cite>. Where riparian soils dominate, lysimeter networks focused in source zones can closely track stream DOC loads; where upland and riparian zones contribute differently, reconcile divergences by quantifying each zone’s share and converting to stream‐integrated loads using discharge and mixing behavior <cite id="3348319a-0">Riparian SOC contents might have a first order control on stream DOC concentrations</cite><cite id="3348319a-0">Riparian soil contributed over 90% of DOC flux in a stream, even though they covered only 6% of the catchment area</cite>. Thus, for carbon budgets, trust the stream gauge for areal‐integral closure and use lysimeters to diagnose and partition sources, adjusting for event vs. baseflow behavior, discharge uncertainty, and analytical footprint differences <cite id="3348319a-4">Daily DOC loads were determined from daily measured discharge data and estimates of linearly interpolated DOC concentration data from approximately weekly DOC concentration measurements for each stream</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-1">One has to carefully consider the discharge data obtained with the handheld flow meter and the uncertainty introduced by the evaluation of the cross-section in the transformation of velocity data to volumes</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-0">The water collected from the lysimeters represents the water and nutrients to which plants have direct access</cite>.

Practical guidance to improve convergence and budget trustworthiness
- Align time scales: pair continuous discharge with frequent concentration sampling; reconstruct daily lysimeter concentration series from campaign means to enable direct flux comparisons within seasons and events <cite id="c6ceb1ac-3">Campaign concentrations were linearly interpolated in time to obtain daily time series of DOC concentrations at each depth and site</cite><cite id="3348319a-4">Daily DOC loads were determined from daily measured discharge data and interpolated weekly concentration data</cite>. 
- Characterize hydrologic separation: map lysimeter footprints and quantify riparian/upland contributions; in systems where riparian soils dominate, focus lysimeter placement in source zones and scale accordingly <cite id="3348319a-0">Dosskey and Bertsch found that riparian soil contributed over 90% of DOC flux in a stream, even though they covered only 6% of the catchment area</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-0">Lysimeters located to best represent the watershed as a whole</cite>. 
- Validate EMC assumptions and event coherence: compare event‐mean soil solution and stream concentrations, assess dilution and variability across discharge ranges, and compute coherence or scaling relationships to identify when EMC is reasonable <cite id="ccb53b9c-2">DOC is highly variable at low flows and exhibits slight dilution at high flows</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-2">Regression slopes for hillslope/lysimeter differ from LMWL and stream water slopes</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-4">Comparisons of coherence are made between stream-pairs within each region without directly comparing method differences</cite>. 
- Quantify discharge uncertainty: calibrate stage–discharge relations, use weirs with known geometry, and propagate uncertainty into load calculations; combine with lysimeter area and concentration uncertainties to estimate budget precision <cite id="3348319a-4">Discharge was recorded continuously using 90° or 120° V-notch or H-flume sharp crested recording weirs and stage-discharge relationships from stilling walls and water-level recorders</cite><cite id="3348319a-1">One has to carefully consider the discharge data obtained with the handheld flow meter and the uncertainty introduced by the evaluation of the cross-section in the transformation of velocity data to volumes</cite>. 
- Treat particulate and analytical factors: where POC is negligible, treat lysimeter TOC as DOC and ensure 0.45 µm filtration and consistent methods across campaigns; interpolate and propagate quality flags through time to avoid bias in daily reconstructions <cite id="c6ceb1ac-1">It has also been shown that boreal surface waters usually carry negligible amounts of particulate organic carbon, making DOC the dominant fraction</cite><cite id="c6ceb1ac-1">Suction lysimeters filter out particles of diameters larger than 1 µm</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-4">Differences in methods between sites are minimized by comparing within-region stream pairs</cite>. 
- Integrate mechanistically: use lysimeter depth profiles to separate horizon‐specific leaching (e.g., O/A horizon vs. B horizon) and convert to areal loads weighted by soil depth/area, then compare with outlet loads; differences reveal storage, bypass, or sorption controls <cite id="ccb53b9c-0">In 1988, 39 zero-tension lysimeters per watershed at 15 sites within each watershed were installed to monitor soil solution volume and chemistry at the bottom of each soil horizon: A, B, and C when possible</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-3">Soil pH, organic matter leaching, and regolith mineralogy are key variables affecting solution chemistry</cite>.

Bottom line
- Lysimeter and stream‐gauge DOC measurements can converge when they sample the same dominant source and integrate over comparable hydrologic regimes and time scales; in many headwaters, lysimeter TOC (as DOC) aligns with stream DOC concentrations because particulate losses are small and riparian soils dominate export, but differences in hydrologic pathways, event vs. baseflow behavior, and integration methods often prevent exact numerical agreement <cite id="c6ceb1ac-1">Riparian soil water TOC concentrations are directly comparable to DOC concentrations in the adjacent streams</cite><cite id="3348319a-0">Riparian SOC content can control stream DOC fluxes; riparian soils contributed over 90% of DOC flux despite 6% area</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-2">Lysimeter and hillslope slopes differ from stream-water LMWL slopes</cite><cite id="ccb53b9c-1">Rewetting and stormflow rapidly transport carbon, reducing in-soil degradation and increasing DOM release</cite>.

Snippet: Stream dissolved organic carbon (DOC) is suggested to be a major constituent of the global carbon cycle [1], [2]. At region to global scales, stream DOC concentrations and flux are largely governed by the quantity and quality of soil organic carbon (SOC). Soil organic carbon storage is an important driver of spatial variation in stream DOC fluxes [3]. At the global scale, DOC flux from watersheds is strongly related to soil C/N ratio [4], and similar relationships hold in some regions [5], [6]. Aitkenhead et al. [7] found that stream DOC concentrations could be predicted by SOC pools at three different scale-catchments with a range of soil types, land use and elevation. At a much smaller scale of investigation, Billett et al. [8] also showed that the spatial pattern of stream DOC concentrations was linked to changes of the SOC content in a small catchment (1.3 km 2 ). At the streamsoil interface, the importance of the riparian zone in controlling carbon flow to the stream has been highlighted by many works [9], [10], [11]. For example, Dosskey and Bertsch [11] found that riparian soil contributed over 90% of DOC flux in a stream, even though they covered only 6% of the catchment area. Therefore, riparian SOC contents might have a first order control on stream DOC concentrations. 

The delivery of SOC to streams can be understood by considering three fundamental processes: (1) partial decomposition of terrestrially fixed carbon producing DOC, (2) hydrologic transport of DOC from the terrestrial environment to streams, and (3) modification of both the quantity and composition of DOC during hydrologic transport [12], [13].
</snippet>

Results indicated a significant influence of discharge on DOC concentrations, shown also in many other studies (Cooper et al., 2007;Grieve, 1994;Hope et al., 1994;Worrall et al., 2002). Cooper et al. (2007) and Worrall et al. (2002) described the importance of the amount of water flowing through soils and its transit time for flushing C out of soils. Title: Soil Aggregates as a Source of Dissolved Organic Carbon to Streams: An Experimental Study on the Effect of Solution Chemistry on Water Extractable Carbon
Snippet: Over the past two decades, headwater streams of the northern hemisphere have shown increased amounts of dissolved organic carbon (DOC), coinciding with decreased acid deposition. The exact nature of the mechanistic link between precipitation composition and stream water DOC is still widely debated in the literature. We hypothesize that soil aggregates are the main source of stream water DOC and that DOC release is greater in organic rich, riparian soils versus hillslope soils. To test these hypotheses, we collected soils from two main landscape positions (hillslope and riparian zones) from the acid-impacted Sleepers River Research Watershed in northeastern Vermont. We performed aqueous soil extracts with solutions of different ionic strength (IS) and composition to simulate changes in soil solution. We monitored dynamic changes in soil particle size, aggregate architecture and composition, leachate DOC concentrations, dissolved organic matter (DOM) characteristics with fluorescence spectroscopy and trends in bioavailability. In low IS solutions, extractable DOC concentrations were significantly higher, particle size (by laser diffraction) was significantly smaller and organic material was separated from mineral particles in scanning electron microscope observations. Furthermore, higher DOC concentrations were found in Na+ compared to Ca2+ solutions of the same IS. These effects are attributed to aggregate dispersion due to expanding diffuse double layers in decreased IS solutions and to decreased bridging by divalent cations. Landscape position impacted quality but not quantity of released DOC. Overall, these results indicate that soil aggregates might be one important link between Critical Zone inputs (i.e. precipitation) and exports in streams.
</snippet>

Prior to sampling, the suction lysimeters were flushed by extracting up to 50 ml of water which were discarded. After flushing, soil water samples were extracted during a period of 24-48 h and collected in acid-washed and pre-evacuated (pressure −1 bar) Milli-Q rinsed Duran glass bottles. The samples were kept dark and cool until they were sub-sampled and frozen for later analysis. The time from sampling to freezing was typically less than 24 h. Soil water TOC was measured by a Shimadzu TOC-5000 using catalytic combustion. The TOC values of the water samples extracted from lysimeter pairs were individually analyzed and then averaged to obtain a single TOC concentration for each of the 5 levels monitored at each site on every sampling occasion. 

It should be noted that suction lysimeters filter out particles of diameters larger than 1 µm. It has also been shown that boreal surface waters usually carry negligible amounts of particulate organic carbon (POC), making dissolved organic carbon (DOC) the dominant fraction (∼ 95 %) of TOC (Laudon et al., 2011).
